Neural operators provide mesh-flexible surrogates for mapping geometry and operating conditions to flow fields; however, in many existing architectures, global parameters such as the freestream state and design variables are concatenated with pointwise inputs, leaving their influence on intermediate features implicit. This paper proposes CoPiT, a \textbf{Co}nditional \textbf{P}osition-induced \textbf{T}ransformer that builds on the Position-induced Transformer (PiT) as its geometric backbone and injects a global condition vector through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), thereby making parametric modulation explicit while preserving geometry-based attention weights. The model is evaluated on two-dimensional AirfRANS airfoil fields, including scarce-data and extrapolation regimes, and on three-dimensional BlendedNet++ blended-wing-body surfaces. On the AirfRANS full-data test set, CoPiT reduces surface and volume losses by approximately 54\% and 24\% relative to Transolver, respectively, and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among the compared baselines on BlendedNet++. Matched ablations show that FiLM conditioning generally improves upon input concatenation, while the preferred placement is task-dependent. CoPiT thus provides a practical operator-learning surrogate for parametric aerodynamics on unstructured meshes.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Personal email agents decide, for every message, what it is, whether it is urgent, whether to draft a reply, create a task, or ignore it. Their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We present Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent in daily use, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, pre-registered hypotheses, human labels in the agent's review loop) that yields ground truth before any training. On 739 real Italian/English emails labelled by the owner (231 unbiased, 500 adversarially sampled), we compare nine systems under thread-grouped cross-validation: the production keyword rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble), a hosted decision model (Nimble v4-max), and hosted generative LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma 4 26B/31B). Four results. The production rules score 28% on message type against a 58% majority class: the field shown most prominently carried no information. With ~200 labels, logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90), though it never predicts the two rarest classes and is statistically tied with Gemma 4 on type; few-shot prompting does not close the gap. The sender's relationship (client, supplier, service) is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy where the contact has been seen, and is not inferable from a single message by any model: it belongs in the contact graph, not the prompt. Finally, accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the most accurate system most often ignores emails needing action (18% vs 4% for the best LLM); a cost-chosen threshold on its noise probability halves that rate and makes it the cheapest system.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 8 pages, 7 tables. Single-user case study. Code and protocol: https://gitlab.com/federicolucca/foyer-measure . The emails are private and not released

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Runtime BiDi Structural Verification Catches Right-to-Left Layout Defects that Accessibility, Actionability, and Logical-Property Linting Miss
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Bidirectional (right-to-left, RTL) layout defects arise when interfaces authored with physical directional CSS (margin-left, border-left, text-align:left) are rendered under dir="rtl" without being mirrored. Accessibility engines (axe-core), actionability engines (Playwright), and even Stylelint's current core logical-property rule fail to localise these defects. We present runtime structural invariants -- a zero-golden mode over computed style and geometry, and a bidi-conservative differential mode -- that catch them in a headless browser. On a held-out benchmark of 14 real RTL bugs reconstructed from dated fix commits in Bootstrap and Material Components Web, the detector recovers 13/14 (2 via zero-golden, 11 via the differential mode), with no false alarm on any patched version; on the actual committed historical bootstrap.rtl.css it catches 1 of 2 attempted. It reports 0 false positives on 16 negative LTR-island cases and, in both modes, on 43 unmodified real components across four design systems and three RTL architectures (rule-of-three 95% upper bound <= 7%), and it surfaced a real directional defect in the current Bulma 1.0.4. By contrast, Stylelint's core rule emits an identical 1744 warnings on Bootstrap's LTR and correct-RTL builds, pseudo-localisation detects none of the mirroring bugs, and a naive pixel mirror-and-diff reaches only F1 0.87 with a test-set-tuned threshold. The two modes are complementary: zero-golden is the sole detector of the decoration/styling-asymmetry class (5/6) but false-flags the correct logical border-inline-end, while the differential detects none of that class yet never false-alarms and is empirically exact on the block-level inset/margin class. We scope this paper to detection; repair is future work.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: STROKE: Simple Sparse Structural Occlusions for Black-Box Adversarial Attacks
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We introduce STROKE, a query-efficient score-based black-box adversarial attack that constructs perturbations from simple oriented rectangular occlusions. STROKE optimizes these perturbations through a lightweight greedy add-and-refine procedure. Across diverse image classifiers, STROKE achieves high attack success with low query counts at nominal 1--2\% area settings, showing favorable performance relative to existing patch-based attacks in several configurations. Matched comparisons further demonstrate substantial reductions in wall-clock attack time, while ablation studies examine the key design choices and effectiveness across structural primitives. These findings suggest that simple structural occlusions offer an effective and computationally efficient search space for black-box adversarial attacks.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, and 16 pages of Supplementary Information with 3 figures and 5 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: What Mean Error Misses: Device-Clock Diagnostics for Evaluating Eye Tracking across Three Virtual Reality Headsets
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Gaze research in virtual reality needs eye trackers of known error. Thirty participants completed the same protocol on the Meta Quest Pro (QP), HTC VIVE Pro Eye (PE) and HTC VIVE Focus Vision (FV); to our knowledge, this is the first evaluation of the FV eye tracker. In a random-saccade task, median participant mean error was 1.04° on QP, 1.50° on PE and 2.41° on FV, which remained least accurate after linear recalibration. In a later block with a darker background, PE error rose by 0.70°. FV samples were positively correlated: dispersion was 9.8 times the sample-to-sample root mean square. The device clocks showed losses that mean error hides. QP paused for up to 6.04 s, and FV skipped single samples. During instructed eye closures, QP flagged every sample valid while gaze moved 9.74°. Evaluations should report repeated timestamps, loss composition on the device clock and validity during eye closures.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 14 pages, 6 figures; supplementary material (16 pages) included. Submitted to ETRA 2027. Data: https://hdl.handle.net/10877/25342 ; code: https://hdl.handle.net/10877/25343

Human-Computer Interaction.title: When Should I Trust This? Designing and Evaluating Factuality Indicators for LLM-based Chatbots
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how people seek information, yet communicating AI factuality to laypeople remains challenging. Through a mixed-methods investigation involving interviews (N=8), a survey (N=1,000), and an experiment (N=5,151), we examine how people evaluate AI-generated information for gardening, mathematical, and medical queries, and how factuality indicators (confidence and sources) shape perceptions. Our interviews and survey show people selectively verify AI responses using external and AI-provided evidence, moderated by contextual factors. Although confidence-indicators affected trust and accuracy perceptions, people hold diverse, ambiguous interpretations of AI confidence. Sources were viewed as crucial, yet users raised concerns about source reliability and verification effort. Our experiment showed that confidence and source-based indicators influenced initial perceptions, but effects disappeared once participants learned the response's correctness. Medical queries elicited skepticism regardless of indicator. Findings motivate helping users interpret model confidence and integrating source information into the interface to support calibrated trust in AI-supported information-seeking.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Beyond pass or fail: an information-processing account of the Turing Test
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The Turing Test is passed when a human interrogator cannot distinguish machine-generated responses from human ones. Yet behavioral indistinguishability can reflect two fundamentally different failures: a failure of encoding, in which machine and human output distributions overlap so closely that source information is effectively absent; or a failure of readout, in which source information is present but the interrogator fails to extract it. To dissociate these possibilities, we inverted the Turing Test, placing humans and AI systems in symmetrical interrogator roles. Using a quantitative information-processing framework, we separated encoding, the information contained in the text; readout, the extraction of that information by an interrogator; and meta-readout, the interrogator's explicit access to the features guiding its own judgments. Across two series of experiments involving more than 3800 human interrogators and two generations of GPT models (GPT-4 and GPT-5), we found a striking dissociation across processing levels and interrogator types. As AI-generated responses became more human-like from GPT-4 to GPT-5, source information became more difficult for human interrogators to extract. GPT-5 interrogators, by contrast, read out source-discriminating information more accurately than GPT-4 interrogators. This improvement, however, came with a specific limitation: GPT-5 explanations only partially aligned with the feature weightings that actually predicted their judgments. Human interrogators showed the complementary pattern, with modest readout alignment but comparatively higher meta-readout alignment. Together, these findings suggest a double dissociation between readout and meta-readout across human and GPT interrogators.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AgentGUI: An Interface for Observing and Steering Long-Running AI Agents
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI agents are increasingly adept at tackling complex, long-running tasks. With the rapid surge of autonomous capabilities, human oversight is systematically lagging behind due to limited human-centered interfacing. Aiming to address this, we introduce AgentGUI, a user-friendly, locally hosted GUI for seamlessly observing and steering AI agents amid multiple concurrent, long-running sessions. AgentGUI features 1) rich agent trajectory visualizations, 2) effective manual and automated steering, and 3) integration with and coordination between open-source and frontier agent frameworks. A controlled user study demonstrates statistically significant reduction in the time it takes to identify key elements from agent traces (38% faster, p = 0.023). In a preliminary experiment, AgentGUI's automated drift prevention feature raises the task completion rate of small local agents by as high as 34pp across a 0.8B--9B model ladder (N=50 runs per model). AgentGUI is publicly available through its project website (https://agent-gui-project.github.io) and open-source repository (https://github.com/eth-medical-ai-lab/agent-gui), along with a demo video (https://youtube.com/watch?v=GSDyxN1gTF0).
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 System Demonstrations

Human-Computer Interaction.title: SPOOK: Sparse Pixel Optimization for Off-Manifold Knowledge in Vision Encoders
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Modern vision encoders are widely used as semantic representations, but the relationship between embedding similarity and human-visible semantics can become unclear far from the natural-image manifold. We probe this regime in a black-box setting by applying sparse pixel edits to blank canvases with a simple pixel-level hill-climbing procedure. Across ImageNet and Flickr30k, we evaluate whether these edited blank canvases can retrieve chosen targets in multimodal contrastive encoders and self-supervised visual encoders. On OpenCLIP, inputs optimized toward class prompts achieve strong top-1 and top-5 targeted retrieval performance; on DINOv3, inputs optimized toward class prototypes achieve high target alignment and near-top prototype ranks. These results show that sparse edits on otherwise blank, visually non-semantic inputs can enter target semantic basins in both language-aligned and self-supervised visual representation spaces. Our findings identify a shared off-manifold failure mode of modern vision encoders and suggest sparse blank-canvas optimization as a simple probe of representation geometry.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables, and 14 pages of Supplementary Material with 8 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Two's a Crowd: Human and AI-Based Copresence for Developers with ADHD
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Effective collaboration and communication are vital to developer productivity and well-being, yet remain constrained by human factors such as attention, intrinsic motivation, and interpersonal accountability. These constraints are particularly vital for developers identifying with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), who navigate persistent environmental barriers in modern hybrid workplace settings. While developers with ADHD frequently rely on collaborative copresence practices (such as body doubling or pair programming) to support executive function, the recent emergence of agentic AI coding assistants has begun reshaping these collaborative dynamics. To investigate how developers with ADHD engage in human and AI-based copresence practices, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 software engineers with ADHD. Our findings reveal that while traditional human-human copresence provides critical social support and onboarding structure, it forces developers to constantly manage professional reputation and sacrifice personal privacy. Conversely, developers leverage emerging human-AI copresence to maintain accountability and cognitive flow without the social anxiety, performance judgment, or surveillance associated with human observation. Based on these empirical insights, we map developer copresence practices onto core dimensions of Goffman's copresence theory and Forsgren et al.'s SPACE framework of developer productivity, and provide design recommendations for AI-based tools that promote inclusive collaboration for developers with ADHD.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 28 pages, 3 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: PAIR-SAFE: A Paired-Agent Approach for Runtime Auditing and Refining AI-Mediated Mental Health Support
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: LLMs are increasingly used for mental health support, yet they can produce responses that are overly directive, inconsistent, or clinically misaligned. Most risk mitigation approaches rely on implicit alignment through training or prompting, offering limited runtime accountability. We introduce PAIR-SAFE, a paired-agent framework that integrates a Responder agent with a Judge agent grounded in the clinically validated Motivational Interviewing Treatment Integrity (MITI-4). The Judge audits each response and issues \allow{} or \revise{} decisions to guide real-time refinement. We evaluate interactions using a support-seeker simulator derived from human-annotated data. The Judge-supervised interactions show significant improvements in key MITI dimensions, including Partnership, Seek Collaboration, and overall Relational quality. Our quantitative findings are corroborated by expert evaluation, highlighting nuances of runtime supervision. Our study reveals that paired-agent auditing can provide clinically grounded, transparent oversight for AI-assisted mental health support.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EMG Tokenization Preserves Movement Information at a Fraction of the Bitrate
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Wireless electromyography (EMG) interfaces must balance electrode coverage against transmission bandwidth. Here, we show that compact EMG tokens substantially reduce payload while retaining information for three-dimensional hand-pose decoding. We evaluate two causal tokenizers fitted without pose labels: an encoder pretrained to reconstruct EMG spectra and one based on SPAR, an engineered spectral-spatial representation of neighbouring electrodes. In personalized, within-session experiments with 320-channel EMG from nine participants, we compare tokenized and continuous features using matched decoder architectures and training procedures. Averaged across decoders, tokenization changed mean error by +0.01 mm for SPAR (95% confidence interval: -0.12 to 0.14) and +0.45 mm for the learned representation (0.10 to 0.82). Both increases met a 1 mm non-inferiority criterion. Stored token arrays reduced payloads 41-fold relative to raw EMG and 36-fold relative to continuous SPAR features. On sampled windows of the public emg2pose benchmark's test partition, absolute differences in mean error between learned tokens and continuous features were below 0.05 mm across 176 participants and in the subset of 20 participants unseen during training. Electrode coverage, calibration, and unseen recordings affected SPAR decoding more than quantization did. In a computational benchmark, optimized SPAR generated tokens for 63 channels within 20 ms on a Cortex-M55 microcontroller. These findings support tokenization as a compact interface between wearable sensing and movement decoding, allowing decoders to be updated while the wearable encoder and transmitted representation remain fixed.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 11 pages, 7 figures; 12-page supplement included. Supplementary Data 1-9 (CSV) are provided as ancillary files

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Political sense-making in "individual" human-technology-world relations: the case of LLM-generated autobiographies
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As AI systems increasingly mediate how people describe, recognize, and present themselves, their politics cannot be reduced to what remains hidden inside the "black box." This chapter argues that AI's political significance emerges within technologically, intersubjectively, and temporally mediated interpretive practices. Bringing Arendt's political philosophy into conversation with Gadamerian hermeneutics, the chapter develops a postphenomenological relational-temporal account of political sense-making across Human-Technology-World relations. Against the charge that postphenomenology remains individualistic and using the case of LLM-generated biographies, the chapter shows how seemingly private human-LLM encounters are worldly and collective. When users ask systems such as ChatGPT to describe them, they do not simply receive algorithmic representations. They interpret, contest, edit, share, and publicly test these descriptions. In doing so, people move interpretively among affective resonance, friction, public re-articulation, and the sedimentation of meaning. This means that the so-called "micro-level" of postphenomenological analysis is already saturated with publicity: affective uptake becomes communicable, reflection becomes accountable, and uses sediment into shared standards of appearance. Simultaneously, we show that once mediation is treated as relational and temporal, the political is not an add-on at the "macro" level; it is intrinsic to the very movement through which technologies amplify and reduce, stabilize and unsettle, and thereby compose a shared world in which judgment can take place. The chapter finishes by discussing several design and policy implications for AI of such political foregrounding in postphenomenology.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Reference: Longo, A., and Kudina, O. (in press). "Political sense-making in 'individual' human-technology-world relations: the case of LLM-generated autobiographies." In D. Michelfelder, & J. Kennedy (Eds.), Postphenomenology Meets Artificial Intelligence. Bloomsbury Academic

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Regulation to Engineering: Organizational Privacy Climate as Mediator
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Data protection legislation aims to protect privacy rights by regulating how information systems store and process personal information. While such legislation defines legal obligations, translating regulatory requirements into engineering practice is far from straightforward. As new frameworks such as the EU AI Act emerge, understanding these mechanisms becomes increasingly relevant. To investigate them, we conducted an online survey of 156 U.S. information system developers, examining the role of organizational privacy climate in the association between developers' perceptions of the GDPR and their privacy engineering practices. Using structural equation modeling, we found that organizational privacy climate mediates the relation between developers' perceived GDPR importance and their privacy attitudes, which in turn are associated with their privacy engineering practices. The mediation chain - regulation, climate, attitudes, practices - complements the direct effect of regulation on practice, revealing the organizational and attitudinal pathway through which regulatory intent reaches engineering behavior. We discuss implications for the next generation of privacy and AI regulation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Perception to Pixels: Human-Derived Visually Distinct Colors for Improved Dominant Color Extraction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Dominant color extraction is a fundamental task in computer vision, with applications in design, image retrieval, and content recommendation. However, conventional algorithms based on device-oriented color spaces (e.g., RGB) and fixed quantization often fail to capture how humans perceive color differences. In this study, we propose a human-perception-based framework for dominant color extraction, built on a novel Human Color Dictionary (HCD) derived from a perceptual experiment. Participants (n=110) were sequentially shown 120 colors and asked to identify those they perceived as unique. Based on their responses, we constructed a 120 by 120 co-occurrence matrix and applied a greedy selection algorithm to derive 64 perceptually distinct colors, forming the HCD. This dictionary was integrated into RGB color histogram and K-means color extraction algorithms by initializing centroids and mapping pixel values to their nearest perceptual color using the deltaE 00 distance. Evaluation on a dataset of 4,562 images paired with expert-designed palettes demonstrated that our method improves perceptual alignment, as measured by Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) and best-match distance. Our findings suggest no meaningful gender differences in the number of uniquely perceived colors, indicating that sex does not significantly influence color perception in this task. Another key finding is that highly saturated colors are perceived as the most distinguishable, whereas dark and deep colors tend to perceptually collapse and are less reliably differentiated. The results confirm that incorporating experimentally derived human color representations ensures the generated color clusters align more closely with human perception, thus improving the usability of color palette generation in practical applications.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CARL: Chat Assisted Reinforcement Learning
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Failure of applied Reinforcement Learning (RL) to solve a given problem predominantly stems from unaddressed specification gaps, where the intent of human experts in the problem's domain is inaccurately or incompletely translated by AI into mathematical objectives, constraints, and reward functions. Failure can also stem from unaddressed performance gaps, where human domain experts are unable to determine the validity of the RL based solution or where parameters (i.e., hyperparameters or weights on the reward terms comprising the reward) are poorly chosen. Chat Assisted Reinforcement Learning (CARL) bridges these gaps through a human-AI co-design interface architecture that enforces interactive specification prior to code generation and then enables subsequent verification and parameter alterations via iteration. More specifically, CARL leads domain experts through a structured ten-step workflow for each iteration using step-specific skill files, domain-aware suggestions via an assistant persona (called Trillian), and compact decision summaries that maintain context across iterations without context overload. Once the domain expert confirms the Markov decision process (MDP) specified by this procedure, CARL's autonomous tool-use loop generates, tests, executes, and debugs an end-to-end RL training pipeline, followed by an interactive post-training diagnosis and revisit step that allows for verification and parameter alteration before running a new iteration if desired.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Revision fixed citation format

Human-Computer Interaction.title: KnowledgeTrail: Understanding Patterns of Exploratory Sensemaking and Serendipitous Discovery in Generative Timelines
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI is reshaping how interactive systems support the discovery and understanding of knowledge, such as how events and ideas developed over time. Yet timelines, one of the most fundamental tools for enabling this kind of temporal sensemaking, remain largely static, limiting user agency and curiosity-driven exploration. Moreover, little is known about how people may explore and make sense of information if the structure of a timeline itself can evolve through interaction. To investigate this question, we designed KnowledgeTrail, a generative timeline that grows and adapts to users' questions, expanding and contracting with their evolving curiosity. Through an exploratory study, we examined how people engage with KnowledgeTrail and identified several patterns of curiosity-driven exploration, serendipitous discovery, and relational sensemaking that differ from conversational AI interfaces. Based on these analyses, our work contributes design implications for future generative systems that support dynamic, user-driven tracing of ideas, events, and their relationships.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Acceptance and Avoidance to Affective Viscosity: Designing Social Agents Intermediating in Human Relationships
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As social agents become embedded in human relationships, they are expected not only to provide smooth assistance but also to handle rejection, discomfort, jealousy, persistence, and other forms of social tension. This paper connects two research directions: acceptance and avoidance in response to an agent's gaze, approach, and contact, and affective viscosity as a model of how negative affect accumulates, persists, is suppressed, and is expressed over time. We argue that avoidance should not be treated merely as a failure of interaction, but as a relational signal that indicates boundaries between humans and agents. Building on this view, affective viscosity provides a design perspective for agents that maintain, suppress, or express negative states depending on social relationships and interaction histories. We discuss several ongoing design cases, including triadic jealousy, discomfort suppression, patience timing, and spatiotemporal stickiness, and consider how these cases lead to broader questions of blame and accountable intervention. Rather than designing agents as simple scapegoats or artificial villains, we ask how agents can intermediate in problematic social situations while making their intervention traceable, limited, contestable, and repairable.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: The 2nd International Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies (TBSA_2nd) in conjunction with HAI 2026, 5 pages, 2 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Virtual Placebo: a scoping review of control conditions in randomized controlled trials of psychological immersive virtual reality interventions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Research on immersive virtual reality (IVR) as a therapeutic tool is growing rapidly, with randomized controlled trials (RCTs) now commonplace. Yet the control conditions in many of these studies that claim strong specific IVR effects vary from usual care to active immersive experiences, making it difficult to draw clinically meaningful conclusions. We conducted a scoping review of recent literature on psychological IVR interventions to assess the main forms of control conditions used and their relations to study outcomes. In this paper, we make the case that most of the recent RCTs studying the effects of specific IVR interventions compare active immersive VR to usual care with no multimedia component. This can lead to strong yet potentially misleading study outcomes and can potentially inflate the IVR interventions' effect. Namely, the lack of an appropriate immersive control condition may risk misattributing general effects of VR devices to the specific content of the intervention. In this review, we discuss the implications of these design choices and propose strategies for including a suitable "virtual placebo" condition to improve the methodological rigor and interpretability of results.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Present Drawing: Exploring Avatar-Mediated Drawing Events with Physical Traces
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We introduce Present Drawing, an approach for staging an avatar-mediated drawing event that leaves physical traces in the real world. Present Drawing aims to reconfigure conventional drawing events by relaxing their physical constraints. We describe an organizer-oriented design space for such an event along four elements: Time, Site, Control Source, and Avatar Embodiment. To ground this concept, we developed a proof-of-concept prototype in which an observer wears a head-mounted display to view an avatar. The avatar's motion is synchronized with a customized pen plotter whose mechanical parts are hidden from the observer. We also developed five application examples spanning live, playback, multi-site, mascot, and system-controlled configurations. We conducted an initial evaluation of one representative playback autograph configuration, showing the basic plausibility of the core Present Drawing experience as an avatar-mediated drawing event and highlighting factors associated with perceiving the avatar as the drawer.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted (ACM UIST 2026)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Forging Emotions: a deep learning experiment on emotions and art
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Affective computing is an interdisciplinary field that studies computational methods that relate to or influence emotion. These methods have been applied to interactive media artworks, but they have focused on affect detection rather than affect generation. For affect generation, computationally creative methods need to be explored that have recently been driven by the use of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), a deep learning method. The experiment presented in this paper, Forging Emotions, explores the use of visual emotion datasets and the working processes of GANs for visual affect generation, that is, for generating images that can convey or trigger specified emotions. This experiment concludes that the methodology used so far by computer science researchers to build image datasets for describing high-level concepts such as emotions is insufficient and proposes utilizing emotional networks of associations according to psychology research. Forging Emotions also concludes that to generate affect visually, merely corresponding to basic psychology findings, such as bright or dark colours, does not seem adequate. Therefore, research efforts should aim to understand the structure of trained GANs and compositional GANs in order to produce genuinely novel compositions that can convey or trigger emotions through the subject matter of generated images.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 10 pages. Published in Artnodes no. 31 (2023), Universitat Oberta de Catalunya, under CC BY 4.0. Extended version of a paper presented at ISEA 2022, Barcelona

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Playing Bias: Epistemic Games for Interpreting Text-to-Image Models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) systems do not merely render prompts; they circulate defaults for "what X looks like," shaping recognition through pose, camera, costume, props, and setting. While technical audits quantify disparities, they rarely cultivate the literacy needed to argue how images assemble stereotypes and confer authority. This paper translates a three-stage, humanities-informed framework into a set of epistemic games that make this cultural work visible and debatable: Interpret (art-historical close looking with AI outputs), Interrogate (counter-intent prompting as artistic exploration), and Expose (creative misuse through paired prompts with a constant motif and a BiasSlot rule, in which only the bias cue varies). In a pilot with undergraduate fine-arts students, the games shifted discussion from impressionistic reactions to concise, warranted hypotheses grounded in visual evidence, supported by lightweight classroom instruments that enabled reproducibility and structured collaboration. We argue that such game-based approaches foster critical literacy across educational contexts, equipping learners to recognize, discuss, and contest how T2I models encode bias.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 11 pages. Accepted at iLRN 2026, the 12th International Conference of the Immersive Learning Research Network, Athens, Greece, June 2026. Video presentation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n_4MiKG5sjw

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Shorter Is Not Cheaper: A Controlled Comparison of Declarative Animation Specifications and Free-Form Code for LLM-Generated Explanations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Chat assistants increasingly answer conceptual questions with interactive, animated explanations, generated either as free-form HTML/JavaScript or as declarative specifications that a fixed runtime plays. The declarative route is widely expected to be cheaper, faster and more reliable, because its outputs are shorter and constrained. We test this expectation in controlled comparisons whose hypotheses and analysis plans were frozen before the runs. We designed ExplainSpec, a time-indexed declarative animation format, and an observation contract that makes every generated explanation programmatically inspectable; validated, pacing-agnostic checkers score 20 explanation requests from five domains. Three Claude models (360 jobs) and, in a follow-up, the open-weight Qwen3-14B with thinking enabled and disabled (240 jobs) answered every request in both formats. For every model the specifications were 25-48% shorter in answer tokens (output excluding reasoning), yet with reasoning enabled total output fell significantly only for the largest Claude model and no model generated significantly faster. The reasons differed. The Claude models reasoned far more before writing specifications (exploratory; for the two larger models, from 15-20% to 85-88% of generations). Qwen3-14B reasoned about as much in both formats (a pre-registered test of this shift was not supported), and its shorter answers saved little against a reasoning trace more than twice as long. Nor were specifications more reliable: free-form pages were valid after one repair round in 95-100% of jobs for every model, whereas Qwen3-14B produced valid specifications in only 33% of jobs and passed all semantic tests in 17% (HTML/JavaScript: 62%). For reasoning models, a shorter format alone therefore does not make generation cheaper, faster or more reliable, and a format learned in context can cost reliability.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Beyond Correctness: How Novice Software Engineering Students Exercise Oversight of Generative AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI (GenAI) is shifting software engineering students' work from producing artefacts towards evaluating and supervising AI-generated outputs. However, little is known about what characteristics students identify in outputs when reporting interventions, or how they exercise oversight during authentic software engineering work. We analysed 962 student-AI interaction turns documented by 145 first-year software engineering students through structured AI Journals, including 172 student-declared interventions. Using a multi-dimensional coding framework, we characterised the output characteristics identified in these reported interventions, students' reasons for intervening, the actions they took, and how those actions were enacted. Fitness problems were identified in 74.4% of interventions, compared with 16.9% involving correctness problems, indicating that oversight more often concerned whether plausible AI outputs were suitable for the engineering task than whether they contained explicit errors. Among classifiable interventions, students most frequently modified generated outputs (51.0%) or refined their prompts (28.2%), with both response types commonly associated with engineering fit. Within-student analysis further showed that outputs perceived as containing minor flaws were associated with lower evaluation confidence than outputs perceived as perfect. Taken together, these findings characterise novice AI oversight as a process that extends beyond error detection to encompass both judgement of fitness for purpose and active intervention in AI-assisted engineering work.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Tool and Trainer? Experimental Evidence on Human Learning from Predictive AI in Cancer Diagnosis
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly deployed to aid professional judgment, yet its implications for the development of human expertise remain unclear. We examine how the availability of AI assistance during training and task execution shapes novices' individual and collective judgment in the context of cancer diagnosis. Across two field experiments at a large teaching hospital, 576 medical novices learned to diagnose lung cancer from CT scans. Study 1 used a 2 * 2 factorial design that randomized AI assistance during training, task execution, both, or neither. Novices who received AI assistance during training achieved higher diagnostic accuracy in both AI-assisted and unaided task execution, with a larger improvement in the former. However, training-phase assistance was associated with more common errors than task-execution-phase assistance, suggesting that while the trainer effect improves individual accuracy, it limits the benefits of aggregating judgments. Study 2 shows that AI assistance during earlier task execution improved subsequent unaided performance and reduced common errors in the unaided phase of task execution, thus revealing a surprisingly beneficial "tool-as-trainer" effect. These findings suggest that, contingent on the right deployment strategy, AI assistance can support individual expertise development and improve collective judgment by reducing common errors across individuals.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Gaze Under Strain: How Oculomotor Behavior Tracks Cybersickness Progression in VR
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Cybersickness remains a major barrier to comfortable, accessible virtual reality (VR). Arising from mismatches between visual and vestibular signals, it places sustained demands on gaze stabilization and visual processing. Because gaze is the mechanism through which users actively sample the virtual environment, cybersickness-induced disruptions may alter both what users perceive and how discomfort itself emerges. Yet, how eye-movement behavior evolves alongside discomfort during prolonged VR exposure remains poorly understood. We present a behavioral analysis of eye-tracking data from 19 participants navigating a realistic virtual environment over a 20-minute session, with discomfort rated repeatedly throughout the experiment. Linear mixed-effects models examined gaze constructs spanning fixation stability, visual exploration, and gaze allocation as functions of discomfort, exposure duration, and their interaction. Our results show that fixation stability degraded progressively with increasing discomfort, with the effect strengthening over time. Visual exploration showed no marginal discomfort effect but exhibited significant discomfort-by-time interactions, indicating that saccadic behavior adapts dynamically rather than responding uniformly to discomfort. Gaze allocation was not associated with discomfort but shifted systematically with time. These findings show that cybersickness does not uniformly disrupt gaze. Instead, different aspects of eye-movement behavior respond differently and change in ways that only become visible when discomfort is tracked repeatedly over time. Understanding how gaze evolves during cybersickness progression provides the behavioral grounding needed to better interpret how discomfort shapes the user's visual experience of immersive environments and to design more sensitive detection approaches.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted for publication at ACM VRST 2026. 10 pages, 4 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CRM-Agent-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using Agents in Stateful Enterprise Environments
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Deploying language agents in real applications demands more than the right answer: an agent must execute a multi-step business process correctly, follow domain-specific rules, and interact with a user across a dialogue, where the gap between saying and doing is the gap between a satisfied customer and a real loss. We argue that a deployable-agent benchmark should jointly assess four facets: the outcome an agent reaches, the trajectory it takes, its operational viability, and its policy compliance. Customer relationship management (CRM), where mutable records meet operational rules and consequential effects, exercises all four. We introduce CRM-Agent-Bench, an execution-grounded benchmark of 555 stateful, multi-turn tasks across nine business domains and 36 capability tags. Each task supplies a task-specific executable contract drawn from checks over actions, arguments, order, response, target state, and protected state; success is the strict conjunction of the checks declared for that task. We evaluate the complete agent system through these contracts and report scored coverage, latency, and cost. Across sixteen systems evaluated on the audited final release, strict success spans 64.32% to 83.60%; the closely grouped leading systems nonetheless diverge sharply in cost and per-domain reliability. CRM-Agent-Bench offers an auditable framework for measuring contract-grounded business-transaction integrity and adherence to task-declared benchmark policies, with a portable structure designed for extension as models improve. Github repository: https://github.com/salesforce-misc/crm-agent-bench
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 52 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "Like Taking the Path of Least Resistance": Exploring the Impact of LLM Interaction on the Creative Process of Programming
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Creativity is fundamentally human. As AI takes on more of the generative work that once required human imagination, despite documented limitations in creative ability, a critical question emerges: How does GenAI affect users' creativity? Through a within-subject study followed by retrospective interviews with (N=20) programmers, we investigated the impact of LLMs on participants' process of creative thinking in programming and the creativity of generated solutions. Across two conditions (LLM-assisted vs. unassisted), participants using LLMs had significantly shorter idea-generation periods (p=0.0004), leading to fewer creative moments (p=0.002). Qualitative analysis of participants' interactions and interviews revealed four different human-LLM collaboration modes supporting various problem-solving strategies. However, a comparative analysis of the generated solutions shows that while LLMs can help generate more correct and functional code, their solutions contain roughly the same number of ideas as participant-generated ones. Based on our findings, we discuss design implications and considerations for effectively using LLMs to support user creativity.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The As-If Machine: Personalized counterfactuals make distant policy risks feel close
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Life experiences can shape policy attitudes, but we only live one life. Citizens may therefore fail to support policies addressing risks they have never personally experienced. Narratives can make such risks immediate and personal, but personalized stories remain difficult to produce at scale. Here we ask whether AI can make distant scenarios feel concrete by simulating a participant's life as if that scenario occurred. We present the As-If Machine (AIM), a multi-agent system through which people co-write personalized counterfactual narratives---stories about their own lives under different policy futures. In two pre-registered and quota-matched experiments on science funding (N=1,007) and satellite cybersecurity (N=894), we compared AIM with two controls: reading an expert-written vignette on the same topic and co-writing with AIM about an unrelated topic. AIM increased psychological closeness---how close a risk feels to the self---by nearly identical margins in the two domains (0.36 and 0.38 standard deviations (SDs) against the vignette, 0.80 and 0.90 against unrelated writing). AIM increased psychological closeness even among participants with unfavorable views of AI. For policy attitudes, AIM's effects were 0.16 SDs against the vignette and 0.10 SDs (n.s.) against unrelated writing for science funding; the corresponding effects for satellite cybersecurity were 0.54 and 0.67 SDs. Across 23,496 human-AI autocomplete interactions, participants and the system played distinct roles: AIM supplied concrete detail that grounded the scenario, and participants supplied first-person perspective and emotion. Co-writing with the As-If Machine makes distant policy risks feel close.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Navigating Deception on Gay Dating Apps: A Qualitative Study of Users' Experiences, Verification Strategies, and Community Knowledge in China
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Gay dating applications have become essential platforms for sexual minority men to seek relationships, intimacy, and community, yet they also expose users to a range of deceptive interactions that remain underexplored in HCI and CSCW research. This study examines how gay male users in China experience, identify, and respond to deception on dating applications. Through semi-structured interviews with 22 participants who used platforms such as Blued, Aloha, Fanka, and Soul, we identify a typology of deceptive practices that users encounter, including relational misrepresentation for sexual access, sustained emotional deception, financial fraud, marketing behavior disguised as ordinary users, and false identity construction. We further analyze the verification and coping strategies that users develop through long-term platform use, such as judging relational intent through interactional pace, identifying financial risk signals, recognizing commercial promotion accounts, and progressively verifying identity authenticity. Finally, we show that risk recognition is not merely an individual capacity but a collaborative practice that gradually emerges through the circulation of experience within the community, the summarization of recurrent deceptive tactics, and the learning of shared rules. Our findings contribute to CSCW scholarship by demonstrating how users of a marginalized community collectively construct practical knowledge about deception, and by revealing that trust assessment on dating platforms operates as a layered, probabilistic, and socially distributed process rather than a binary judgment.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to ACM GROUP 2027

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Whale You Go Green? Immediate and Longitudinal Effects of Embodied Conversational AI Avatars on Sustainable Behavioral Tendencies and Pro-Environmental Attitudes
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Embodied conversational AI can be persuasive, but can it motivate people to develop sustainable behavioral tendencies and increase pro-environmental attitudes? We conducted a randomized experiment (N = 576) comparing four embodied avatars--a beluga whale, Greta Thunberg, Emma Watson, and a generic human--with a text chatbot and no-intervention control. All embodied conditions increased immediate sustainable product selection relative to the control (beta = .401-.609, all q <= .0126) and chatbot (beta = .398-.604, all q <= .007), without differing significantly from one another. Only the Beluga condition increased immediate pro-environmental attitudes relative to the control after correction. Among 287 returners assessed two months later, following an intermediate assigned-condition session, Beluga also showed significantly higher pre-booster sustainable product choice compared to the control (beta = .657, q = .0176). Although it did not significantly outperform other embodied agents, these findings establish the immediate potential of nonhuman embodied avatar interfaces as a promising direction for memorable environmental interventions.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "You Already Have Me--Why Do You Still Use Blued?" How Gay Dating Apps Shape Intimate Relationships Among Chinese Gay Men
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Gay dating applications such as Blued are widely used for meeting partners, yet their role does not end once an intimate relationship is formed. When these platforms persist within an established relationship, they transform from matchmaking tools into a form of relational infrastructure that both partners must continuously manage. Building on existing CSCW and HCI research that has primarily examined how social media triggers jealousy, surveillance, or trust issues in intimate relationships, this study investigates how the persistent presence of gay dating applications shapes the dynamics of intimate relationships among Chinese gay men. Through semi-structured interviews with 23 self-identified gay men aged 19 to 55, we identify a recurring cyclical process: platform signals-such as online status, profile updates, distance indicators, and usage records-trigger suspicion and conflict; partners invest negotiation labor through intent explanation, visibility control, rule formation, or silence; and these negotiations eventually sediment into temporary governance settlements that reduce trigger frequency but remain conditionally stable. We identify four types of governance settlements: infrastructure removal, transparency governance, silence agreements, and layered/open agreements. Each settlement addresses the governance problems of platform presence, visibility distribution, and loyalty boundaries differently, yet none achieves permanent stability due to platforms' reversible entry mechanisms and continuous visibility cues. Our findings extend existing CSCW research on digital technology and intimate relationships by revealing a more complex process than previously documented: platform signals not only trigger emotional responses but prompt partners to engage in sustained relational negotiation through explanation, visibility management, rule formation, or silence.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to ACM GROUP 2027

Human-Computer Interaction.title: GlanceAR: Repurposing Phone Sensors via Low-Cost Reflectors for Always-On Obstacle Awareness
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Smartphone use while walking reduces environmental awareness and can lead to accidents and injury, yet existing obstacle-awareness systems remain unadopted because they require users to hold the phone upright and aimed forward, conflicting with how people actually hold their devices. We introduce GlanceAR, an always-on mobile obstacle-awareness system designed for natural phone-holding postures. GlanceAR utilizes a low-cost passive mirror attachment to redirect the phone's rear LiDAR and RGB camera forward without additional electronic components. In a within-subjects study with N=11 participants navigating indoor and outdoor obstacle courses while engaged in a primary on-phone task, we evaluated three sensing configurations: GlanceAR, a LiDAR-only variant for privacy, and an attachment-free ultra-wide camera baseline. Our findings reveal trade-offs among sensing fidelity, obstacle cue design, and social acceptability, and surface insights around AI complacency and the tension between on-screen task focus and physical safety.

Software Engineering.title: Runtime BiDi Structural Verification Catches Right-to-Left Layout Defects that Accessibility, Actionability, and Logical-Property Linting Miss
Software Engineering.summary: Bidirectional (right-to-left, RTL) layout defects arise when interfaces authored with physical directional CSS (margin-left, border-left, text-align:left) are rendered under dir="rtl" without being mirrored. Accessibility engines (axe-core), actionability engines (Playwright), and even Stylelint's current core logical-property rule fail to localise these defects. We present runtime structural invariants -- a zero-golden mode over computed style and geometry, and a bidi-conservative differential mode -- that catch them in a headless browser. On a held-out benchmark of 14 real RTL bugs reconstructed from dated fix commits in Bootstrap and Material Components Web, the detector recovers 13/14 (2 via zero-golden, 11 via the differential mode), with no false alarm on any patched version; on the actual committed historical bootstrap.rtl.css it catches 1 of 2 attempted. It reports 0 false positives on 16 negative LTR-island cases and, in both modes, on 43 unmodified real components across four design systems and three RTL architectures (rule-of-three 95% upper bound <= 7%), and it surfaced a real directional defect in the current Bulma 1.0.4. By contrast, Stylelint's core rule emits an identical 1744 warnings on Bootstrap's LTR and correct-RTL builds, pseudo-localisation detects none of the mirroring bugs, and a naive pixel mirror-and-diff reaches only F1 0.87 with a test-set-tuned threshold. The two modes are complementary: zero-golden is the sole detector of the decoration/styling-asymmetry class (5/6) but false-flags the correct logical border-inline-end, while the differential detects none of that class yet never false-alarms and is empirically exact on the block-level inset/margin class. We scope this paper to detection; repair is future work.

Software Engineering.title: Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations
Software Engineering.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to optimize code for performance. This practice often assumes that improvements in execution speed naturally translate into overall lower energy consumption. We challenge this assumption empirically by measuring whether performance-optimized code produced by LLM self-refinement pipelines is also energy-efficient relative to canonical human reference solutions, and whether the energy cost of the optimization process can be offset by subsequent execution-time savings. We evaluate 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on all 1,000 problems of EffiBench, a state-of-the-art performance benchmark, while collecting per-process, hardware-level energy measurements throughout. Inference energy spans 0.79 to 8.68 MJ across model-variant pairs, which is roughly equivalent to the energy of 250 to 2800 GPT-4.1 queries. Limiting the maximum number of output tokens has the largest impact, reducing energy use by up to 69% compared to the default configuration. On the execution side, 42 of 44 configurations produce code that consumes more energy per problem than the canonical human reference, with overheads ranging from +4% to +886%. The two exceptions achieve only marginal gains, with break-even points on the order of 10^6 to 10^7 executions. Mixture-of-Experts architectures consume substantially less inference energy than equivalently-sized dense models without sacrificing correctness, making architectural choice a more consequential sustainability lever than decoding parameters. Performance optimization and energy efficiency are not always aligned goals: LLM self-refinement consistently produces faster-seeking but energy-heavier code relative to what a human engineer would write. All artifacts are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598170.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027)

Software Engineering.title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
Software Engineering.summary: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way.
Software Engineering.comment: 33 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to IEEE Access. Code: https://github.com/lzh0082-cloud/CODE-DETECTION

Software Engineering.title: Two's a Crowd: Human and AI-Based Copresence for Developers with ADHD
Software Engineering.summary: Effective collaboration and communication are vital to developer productivity and well-being, yet remain constrained by human factors such as attention, intrinsic motivation, and interpersonal accountability. These constraints are particularly vital for developers identifying with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), who navigate persistent environmental barriers in modern hybrid workplace settings. While developers with ADHD frequently rely on collaborative copresence practices (such as body doubling or pair programming) to support executive function, the recent emergence of agentic AI coding assistants has begun reshaping these collaborative dynamics. To investigate how developers with ADHD engage in human and AI-based copresence practices, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 software engineers with ADHD. Our findings reveal that while traditional human-human copresence provides critical social support and onboarding structure, it forces developers to constantly manage professional reputation and sacrifice personal privacy. Conversely, developers leverage emerging human-AI copresence to maintain accountability and cognitive flow without the social anxiety, performance judgment, or surveillance associated with human observation. Based on these empirical insights, we map developer copresence practices onto core dimensions of Goffman's copresence theory and Forsgren et al.'s SPACE framework of developer productivity, and provide design recommendations for AI-based tools that promote inclusive collaboration for developers with ADHD.

Software Engineering.title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges
Software Engineering.summary: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-based framework that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and expected score relations for each. SANE also defines a scorer-independent validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its expected relation. Because SANE generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, SANE produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (JRH) at comparable end-to-end validity and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain, including professionalism and toxicity, where JRH detects none. On faithfulness, SANE achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman rho = 0.852), while JRH does not (rho = 0.100).
Software Engineering.comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. A shorter version was accepted for presentation at the non-archival NeurIPS 2026 TAE workshop

Software Engineering.title: OpenDraco: A Platform for Engineering and Experimenting with Configurable Multi-Agent Architectures for Software Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Experimenting with LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) involves an iterative cycle of modeling configurations, executing and evaluating them, comparing results, and refining system designs. Existing approaches provide limited end-to-end support for this experimentation lifecycle. We present OpenDraco, an open-source platform that integrates these activities into a single workflow. OpenDraco represents agents, prompts, tools, models, parameters, and communication topology in exportable, versioned JSON specifications, translated into executable LangGraph workflows supporting different interaction structures. Users can modify and re-evaluate configurations using local or cloud-based LLMs. We instantiate OpenDraco for automated program repair (APR) and evaluate a sequential baseline and seven reconstructed configurations on synthetic and real-world SWE-bench Lite issues. The results reveal substantial cost differences among configurations with similar repair outcomes, while the baseline resolves 12 of 77 SWE-bench issues using open-source LLMs. Additional proof-of-concept tasks illustrate applicability beyond APR. OpenDraco supports iterative experimentation with heterogeneous MAS configurations, enabling researchers to examine their outcomes and costs within a common environment. Demonstration video: https://youtu.be/278sOR4lBEk.

Software Engineering.title: CC4Q Workbench: From Quantum Repositories to Analyzable Code Comments
Software Engineering.summary: Quantum software development kits (SDKs) expose high-level APIs whose use requires an understanding of underlying mathematical principles, circuit semantics, and hardware properties. Code comments can provide natural-language or structural explanations that are not explicit in API calls. However, studying comments in a new quantum SDK still requires researchers to coordinate separate steps for comment extraction, quantum-specific classification, and manual verification, resulting in repeated integration effort. To address this problem, we present CC4Q Workbench, an open-source workbench that integrates these steps into a reusable workflow. Given a Python repository at a specified revision, CC4Q Workbench automatically extracts code-comment pairs, segments comments into sentence-level units, and applies two trained classifiers to identify quantum-specific content and assign quantum-knowledge categories. Its web interface supports exploration of bundled datasets, inspection of code snippets, corpus construction from new repositories, manual annotation with model predictions hidden during binary labeling, and classifier fine-tuning using exported annotations. The release provides aggregate statistics for six SDK datasets comprising 39,593 sentence-level code comment units (SCCUs), of which 17,517 are browsable in the web interface. Applied to three additional application-layer Qiskit repositories outside the original CC4Q dataset, the pipeline ran without code changes and produced 11,517 SCCUs. Manual verification of 379 SCCUs showed 85.0% agreement between human annotations and the binary classifier's predictions.

Software Engineering.title: StateMirror: Pre-Execution Detection of Hallucinated Tool Calls in Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based coding agents may propose invalid actions that are not applicable in the execution environment, such as accessing non-existent paths or missing packages. We term this mismatch hallucinated tool use. A preliminary study of 4,398 agent trajectories reveals that these hallucinations are pervasive and costly, requiring a median of 3 additional interaction steps and 22.4K tokens to recover. Existing frameworks rely on reactive, post-execution feedback, wasting runtime resources. Nevertheless, since an agent's execution environment is grounded in concrete codebase and harness components, many action prerequisites can be extracted and validated prior to execution. To this end, we introduce StateMirror, a lightweight pre-execution detector. StateMirror intercepts actions at the harness boundary, extracts state predicates via AST and command analysis, and deterministically validates them against the live repository. By pinpointing exact environment mismatches before execution, StateMirror preempts invalid actions and subsequent recovery cycles. Evaluation on 2,508 actions shows StateMirror achieves 0.940 precision and 0.817 F1 in detecting such hallucinations, surpassing the strongest LLM judge by 35.3% in F1 while reducing median detection latency from 17.73 s to 1.50 ms with zero token consumption. For practical mitigation, StateMirror's pre-execution feedback enables agents to rectify over 95% of hallucinated tool calls. During live mitigation on 79 tasks, StateMirror reduces agent execution time by 15.8% and token consumption by 11.8% while maintaining task resolution.

Software Engineering.title: Can AI Agents Help Robotic Engineers? Lessons from Two Focus Days in Industry
Software Engineering.summary: Software developers increasingly use AI agents that execute multi-step programming tasks on their own. However, it is unclear if and how this transfers to robotic engineering, where engineers program industrial robots in niche, vendor-specific languages and rely on visual feedback from simulation tools. Within this paper, we report a case study on the use of AI agents by an SME that programs industrial robots. Our results show that the agent did not make the engineers more productive, with the exception of a task that required the generation of highly repetitive code. However, the results with the agent improved over time, as the engineers learned how to use it and the agent was adapted to the domain. Moreover, the experience with AI mattered more for the success with the agent than the experience with robotic engineering. This shows that AI agents are not a plug-and-play solution. Instead, companies must train their engineers on the usage of agents, plan time for a learning curve, and ensure that agent configurations match the domain and developer requirements. The strong learning curve we observed further implies that studies on productivity gains with AI should be longitudinal, as they otherwise miss how engineers adopt agents in practice.

Software Engineering.title: Automated Multi-Line Bug Repair Using Model Checker Aided LLMs: A Case Study on RISC-V Processors
Software Engineering.summary: Functional verification of Register-Transfer Level(RTL) designs has become a critical bottleneck in modern semiconductor development, often consuming the majority of project resources. Debugging, in particular, remains an especially time-consuming task, requiring careful analysis of simulation traces or counterexamples. Recent work has explored applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to RTL debug and repair with great promise. However, the existing approaches typically are for single-line bugs, operate in open-loop, rely heavily on prompts or retrieval, lack scalability, and often produce incorrect fixes. In this paper, we propose a novel automated RTL bug repair methodology that combines LLMs, assertions, and a model checker to provide scalable, trustworthy semantic grounding and formal guarantees. Concretely, the methodology leverages failing assertions to guide the LLM in generating patches for multi-line bugs. Each candidate patch is formally verified using a model checker (JasperGold), ensuring only valid repairs are accepted. We evaluate the efficacy and scalability of our methodology on the BRISC-V RISC-V core using mutation testing, introducing several mutation types, and demonstrate that our methodology can repair up to 98% of single-line RTL bugs and 93% of the multi-line bugs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show automated, LLM-assisted RTL multi-line bug repair results on a complex RISC-V processor design in a scalable manner.

Software Engineering.title: Lessons Outlive Their Failures: A Case Study of Rules for AI Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: AI coding agents increasingly work inside a harness: rule files such as AGENTS.md, on-demand skills, runtime hooks and automated checks. Most studies of harnesses look at a single point in time or at short benchmark runs. I report a six-week case study of my personal system of record, a plain-markdown repository that three AI agent tools edited daily under one shared rule set. I built a ledger of 118 agent failures, their fixes and whether they came back. I also tested the system's monthly LLM documentation audit against 47 known stale statements and 20 planted errors. Finally, I replayed five past failures in isolated git clones, with and without their fixes. All results come from one repository with three runs per condition, so I report them as exploratory. Stale documentation (drift) was the largest failure class (48 of 118), although 35 of those were found on one audit day. A single audit run found about half of the known drift (Claude Sonnet 5.5 mean: 50%), and at least 93% of its findings were correct. On Sonnet 5.5, the agent finished four of the five replayed tasks. In three of those four, the failure did not happen, with or without its fix. Only the stale-count failure came back without its check, and the check stopped it in every run. On older models, an agent drafted an em-dash once while the em-dash lint check was active, and the check rejected it. A written rule on run-time estimates did not change Sonnet 4.5's overestimates. These results suggest that harness lessons can outlive the failures they were written to fix, while drift persists and still needs mechanical checks. Tools that evolve a harness add lessons faster than they retire them, so they should re-test their rules from time to time and retire the obsolete ones.

Software Engineering.title: From Regulation to Engineering: Organizational Privacy Climate as Mediator
Software Engineering.summary: Data protection legislation aims to protect privacy rights by regulating how information systems store and process personal information. While such legislation defines legal obligations, translating regulatory requirements into engineering practice is far from straightforward. As new frameworks such as the EU AI Act emerge, understanding these mechanisms becomes increasingly relevant. To investigate them, we conducted an online survey of 156 U.S. information system developers, examining the role of organizational privacy climate in the association between developers' perceptions of the GDPR and their privacy engineering practices. Using structural equation modeling, we found that organizational privacy climate mediates the relation between developers' perceived GDPR importance and their privacy attitudes, which in turn are associated with their privacy engineering practices. The mediation chain - regulation, climate, attitudes, practices - complements the direct effect of regulation on practice, revealing the organizational and attitudinal pathway through which regulatory intent reaches engineering behavior. We discuss implications for the next generation of privacy and AI regulation.

Software Engineering.title: Tool-Calling LLM Agents Under Realistic MCP Faults: Scale Does Not Purchase Fault Tolerance
Software Engineering.summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), yet current benchmarks assume tools respond correctly and on time, leaving agent resilience to realistic tool failures untested. We introduce MCP-Injector, a drop-in, protocol-aware fault-injection middleware that interposes on the MCP tool-call path with controlled persistence (permanent, transient, intermittent) and seedable schedules. Its fault model is calibrated to the observed incident distribution (failure mode x persistence) of the public MCP ecosystem, mined from 57,240 issue and pull-request threads across 1,774 open-source MCP repositories. In a 1,350-cell experiment crossing two backbone sizes (20B, 120B), three agent stacks (custom multi-round plan-and-execute, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain), and three fault injection conditions, we find that faults drawn from this permanent-heavy stress profile cause severe quality degradation (task-completion score falls by 60%, from 8.08 to 3.23 out of 10), and that scale does not purchase fault tolerance for the two gpt-oss backbones we test: the 120B retains no larger share of its fault-free score under faults (resilience-ratio model, $p = 0.96$), and its completion rate under faults is, if anything, lower (91.1% vs. 95.6%; difference 4.4 points, 95% CI $[-0.2, 9.3]$). Agent stacks differ in how well they absorb faults, which suggests that framework-level error handling matters more than model scale. These results demonstrate that capability benchmarks alone can mask operational brittleness, motivating protocol-aware fault injection as a complementary evaluation dimension for tool-calling agents.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). 10 pages of main text plus appendices and the NeurIPS checklist. Code and data: https://gitlab.com/uniluxembourg/snt/sedan/papers/mcp-injector (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23573765)

Software Engineering.title: Beyond Coverage and Mutation: A Blind-Spot Analysis of LLM-Generated Unit Tests
Software Engineering.summary: Existing evaluation protocols for unit tests rely on aggregate metrics such as branch coverage and mutation score. These metrics quantify the extent to which a test suite exercises program behavior, but do not identify the behavioral obligations it systematically leaves unchecked. We propose BlindSpotEval, an obligation-based evaluation framework aligned with the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern. The framework comprises three metrics, Boundary-Value Adequacy, Control-Flow Adequacy, and Oracle Strength, complemented by an assessment of execution reliability. We also introduce ObligBench, a complexity-stratified Java benchmark comprising 895 complex and 700 low-complexity functions with source-side obligation annotations. Evaluating 14,320 tests from four LLMs under four prompting strategies reveals systematic blind spots. Incorrect assertions account for 15.6% of test failures, illustrating that coverage alone does not establish oracle correctness. Among executable tests, coverage of null, negative, and empty arguments reaches only 34.8%, 23.8%, and 38.8%, compared with average coverage above 93% for booleans. Catch blocks and default groups have Control-Flow Adequacy scores of only 0.100 and 0.312. Across both dimensions, LLM-generated tests exhibit the happy-path bias observed in human-written tests, concentrating on normal inputs and expected flows while leaving unusual values and exceptional paths unchecked. Oracle strength is high on average but uneven, with weaker assertions for object return property values and exceptions. These blind spots also occur in low-complexity functions, suggesting that code complexity alone does not explain them.
