Software Engineering.summary: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. In this paper, we present SecPRBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic security review on validated real-world code changes. More specifically, we have built an automated agentic pipeline to autonomously harvest, build, and validate massive real-world bug-introducing commits for popular software systems. To ensure precise evaluation, we also adopt LLM-as-a-judge to credit the findings matching ground-truth vulnerabilities. To date, we have collected 265 tasks from nine critical systems, including Firefox, V8, and OpenSSL with millions of lines of code. Across eight frontier models, recall ranges from 32.5% to 78.1%, with Grok 4.6 and GPT-6 sol ranking at the top. Our study also shows that most misses are not simply oversights: in 68% of them, the agent reports on a file that holds the flaw but argues for a different mechanism. Security-focused harnesses also behave differently: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers recall by 8.3 points, mostly by abstaining, while Anthropic's Defending Code harness raises it by 7.7 points, at a higher cost.
Software Engineering.comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Benchmark: https://github.com/secprbench/secprbench Results website: https://secprbench.github.io

Software Engineering.title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization
Software Engineering.summary: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.
Software Engineering.comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Code, pre-registrations, and 1,750 run logs at https://github.com/shangliy/lineage-is-memory

Software Engineering.title: One Verdict Is Not Enough: Regression Testing Learned World Models and Their Test Harnesses
Software Engineering.summary: Learned world models ship as software components whose model versions, preprocessing, and test harnesses change between releases. Work on model updates already counts per-sample regressions, or negative flips, that an accuracy check hides. Two problems remain: a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce erroneous scores and wrong verdicts without a crash. We present TetraState, a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests. Each test runs under four fixed model-native configurations; its number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes. Inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate. Revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test. On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests and two heterogeneous systems, Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels; in the second, accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correctly, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, so a modal-verdict flip check misses them. These results outline a research agenda on configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.

Software Engineering.title: RepGen: Reproducing Deep Learning Bugs through Context-Aware Code Generation and Verification
Software Engineering.summary: Reproducing deep learning (DL) bugs is challenging because failures can involve source code, models, data, dependencies, and execution environments. Incomplete bug reports further complicate reproduction by omitting essential details. We present RepGen, an open-source tool for reproducing DL bugs through context-aware code generation and iterative verification. Given a bug report and repository, RepGen explores the codebase to build a learning-enhanced context, develop a reproduction plan, and generate candidate scripts. It refines candidates using static checks and LLM feedback to improve their correctness and relevance. When enabled, the tool prepares the execution environment, runs the script, and assesses its output against the reported failure. RepGen provides an interactive command-line interface supporting local and hosted LLMs, configurable execution budgets, and inspectable artifacts, along with a GitHub Action for automated issue processing. The underlying approach reproduced 85 of 106 real-world DL bugs (80.19%). A controlled study with 27 developers showed a 23.35% improvement in reproduction success and a 56.8% reduction in reproduction time.
Software Engineering.comment: Under Review - ICSE 2027 Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase Track

Software Engineering.title: AIFaultBench: A Reproducible Benchmark of Real-World Faults in AI Software Systems
Software Engineering.summary: AI-based software systems remain difficult to debug because their failures can involve interactions among code, models, data, dependencies, hardware, and execution environments. Existing benchmarks cover specific classes of AI systems, while concerns about fault realism and reproducibility highlight the need for documented execution conditions and evidence. We present AIFaultBench, a benchmark of 770 real-world bugs from 105 AI-based software repositories across 76 organizations. It covers six classes of AI systems: machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, systems based on large language models, agentic AI, and AI tooling and infrastructure. Each bug record connects the original report and affected codebase to structured metadata, environment setup scripts, a reproduction trigger, and investigation evidence. We reproduced 652 bugs (84.7%) under the recorded execution conditions and documented the outcomes of the remaining 118 attempts. Through its broad coverage, documented reproduction evidence, and common structure, AIFaultBench supports empirical studies of AI faults, debugging tool evaluation, practical failure investigation, and teaching with real-world examples.
Software Engineering.comment: Under Review - ICSE 2027 Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase Track

Software Engineering.title: Isomorphism Is Not Enough: An Agentic Audit of Verified Code Generation in Lean
Software Engineering.summary: Agentic systems have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for automated theorem proving in formal mathematics. To assess how far these capabilities extend to program verification and how reliably existing benchmarks can measure them, we audit CLEVER, a Lean 4 benchmark for verifiable code generation, using three independent agentic stacks based on Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.5. Our audit finds arguably erroneous reference specifications in 80 of 161 entries, each accepted by the benchmark's authors, distills a taxonomy of benchmark errors, and exposes structural limitations of isomorphism-based scoring, whose signal breaks down when generated and reference specifications formalize different yet defensible readings. In the process, the stacks generate arguably valid specifications for up to 98.8% of entries, certify implementations against sound reference specifications for up to 92.3%, and reach up to 96.2% end-to-end success over entries with sound premises, suggesting that CLEVER no longer stresses modern agentic provers as much as its design intended. Looking ahead, we translate our findings into recommendations for future work, with our error analysis doubling as a repair list for CLEVER and a heuristic checklist for the next generation of benchmarks.

Software Engineering.title: Automatically Enhancing the Quality of Android App Bug Reports
Software Engineering.summary:
Most defects in mobile applications are visually observable on the device screen. Since automated mechanisms for detecting and reporting such defects are often unavailable, users, testers, and developers must manually submit bug reports. However, these reports are frequently incomplete, ambiguous, or inaccurate, often lacking the information needed to understand, reproduce, and diagnose defects.
  We formulate automatic bug report enhancement as the problem of connecting user-written bug reports with application execution. We present BUGSCRIBE, an LLM-powered approach that links bug report information with app-specific UI execution information to infer and generate accurate, complete, and correct Observed Behavior (OB), Expected Behavior (EB), and Steps to Reproduce (S2Rs). To support BUGSCRIBE's design and evaluation, we develop a bug report quality model and use it to identify the most effective context for each component. We evaluate BUGSCRIBE on 48 bug reports from 26 Android applications with manually constructed ground truth. Our results show that BUGSCRIBE generates higher-quality bug report components than the original reports and three LLM-based baselines, improving S2R quality by 44.2%--84.7%, and OB/EB quality by up to 35.2%. We further show that BUGSCRIBE-generated reports help an LLM-based agent reproduce Android bugs, improving the reproduction rate by 28.1%--57.7% compared to the original reports and the baselines.

Software Engineering.title: Trellis: Bringing Compiler-Guided Repair into Agentic Code Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents regularly generate programs that do not compile and require substantial tokens to repair. Yet most repairs are small and local to the edit that caused them. We present Trellis, a system that integrates incremental compiler feedback into code generation to improve code correctness while controlling repair costs. Trellis uses rollback-based search for targeted repair and asynchronous checking and checkpointing for efficient execution. We adapt Clang and tsc to Trellis's checker interface and integrate Trellis transparently into OpenCode. On C/C++ and TypeScript software engineering tasks, Trellis improves compilation rate by up to 13% and test pass rate by up to 11% with comparable token consumption to baseline OpenCode.

Software Engineering.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.

Software Engineering.title: TRAIL: Towards Effective Log Parsing for Rare Logs through Template-Preserving Augmentation
Software Engineering.summary: Log parsing is essential for system log analysis because it supports tasks such as debugging, monitoring, and anomaly detection by transforming unstructured log messages into structured log templates. However, real-world log datasets exhibit highly imbalanced, long-tailed distributions, where a small number of frequent templates dominate while many rare templates appear only a few times. This imbalance causes evaluation results to be overly optimistic by allowing frequent templates to dominate benchmark metrics, while poor performance on rare yet operationally important events remains largely hidden. In this paper, we investigate the prevalence and impact of rare log groups, defined as log groups with fewer than five instances. Our empirical study on the widely used Loghub-2.0 benchmark shows that rare log groups account for nearly 20% of all templates but less than 0.01% of log messages. Because they contain only a handful of instances, all evaluated parsers experience substantial performance degradation on these groups. To address this challenge, we propose TAILOR, a log parsing framework that improves template inference for rare log groups through template-preserving augmentation. TAILOR enriches rare log groups with template- consistent log messages before template inference. The additional structural evidence helps distinguish static tokens from dynamic variables. Our experimental results show that TAILOR improves parsing accuracy on rare log groups by 19% over the strongest baseline while maintaining competitive performance on complete datasets. We further show that the proposed augmentation strategy generalizes across different LLM backbones and consistently improves existing LLM-based parsers without modifying their core architectures.

Software Engineering.title: Agent Stack for ML Training Lifecycle: Generation, Validation, and Optimization
Software Engineering.summary: Production model development requires repeated architecture design, platform integration, debugging, training, and evaluation. We present an agent stack deployed at LinkedIn with two independently usable agent loops: AutoTorch for model generation and migration, and AutoResearch for model optimization. AutoTorch generates PyTorch models and training pipelines for TensorFlow migration, XGBoost replacement, and new-model development. Executable validation hooks check platform API compliance, trainability, and conversion fidelity on sampled data, guiding iterative repair before engineer review and full-scale distributed training. AutoResearch explores architecture and training-configuration changes through expert-steered or autonomous experimentation. An external orchestrator manages parallel trials, experiment history, candidate selection, and wall-clock budgets across agent sessions. A shared runtime preserves execution state independently of agent reasoning and allocates GPUs separately from agent execution. Across ranking, content understanding, and recommendation workloads, AutoTorch completed generation and full-scale training in 92 of 115 workflow runs (80%). Of these, 77 (83.7%) produced models meeting post-training quality requirements. In a separate cohort, AutoResearch improved the primary task metric on held-out data for 28 of 100 production pipelines. Engineering teams estimate that the stack reduced elapsed end-to-end migration time from approximately eight weeks to two weeks, a 4x speedup.

Software Engineering.title: Autoformalization for Ambiguous Inputs: Precision, Coverage, and Cost across SQL and Logical Forms
Software Engineering.summary: Agentic systems translate natural-language requests into executable artifacts while managing ambiguity and inference cost. We evaluate seven autoformalization workflows on SQL and first-order logic benchmarks for ambiguous inputs. Across five SQL workflows, the raw model leads with F1 of 53.35% on AMBROSIA and 60.85% on AmbiQT. On AmP, DRIFT gains 15.98 F1 points over the raw model at 2.03 times its token cost, whereas LoC uses 18.65 times the raw model's tokens with lower F1. Within AutoCedar, structured interpretation lowers F1 by 6.44-6.95 points and raises AMBROSIA token use 2.2-fold. Paired reviewer comparisons show modest Kimi K3 gains of 1.93 points on AMBROSIA and 2.04 on AmbiQT. Clear-ambiguous AMBROSIA analysis shows greater relative stability for AutoCedar, with a smaller F1 drop than the raw model (11.46 vs. 16.68 points), alongside lower aggregate F1 (50.16% vs. 53.35%). Autoformalization alone does not guarantee robustness to ambiguity: the tested additions offer no uniformly effective remedy, making accuracy, ambiguity handling, and inference cost joint design requirements.

Software Engineering.title: Hardware-Aware Conditional Code in Android Apps
Software Engineering.summary:
Android OS runs on a highly diverse set of devices, spanning entry-level phones and flagships with substantially different hardware characteristics, including memory capacity, processors, displays, cameras, and sensors. Through APIs, apps can query device information at runtime, such as memory, hardware features, and manufacturer, among other device properties, allowing developers to execute different code paths on different devices. Existing studies cover only specific compatibility bugs or brand-specific behavior; however, the broader use of hardware information in app logic has not been comprehensively explored.
  We address this question with a large-scale empirical study of hardware-related if statements in Android apps. We statically analyze 50,000 apps to identify the if statements whose conditions depend on the values of hardware-related APIs, and extract their conditions together with the code of their branches. Our results show that 95% of successfully analyzed apps contain at least one such statement, with an average of 74 per app, which suggests that hardware-related logic is widespread. We then apply an LLM-assisted open-coding process to the extracted code to build a structured taxonomy of the purposes behind hardware-related conditional code. The resulting characterization shows that developers use hardware information for feature availability checks, UI adaptation, emulator detection, device tiering, and resource management, among others.

Software Engineering.title: Software Change Request in AI-Orchestrated Software Evolution: Literature Review and Research Agenda
Software Engineering.summary: In the emerging paradigm of holistic AI-orchestrated software maintenance and evolution, large-scale app stores continuously generate exponentially vast Software Change Requests (SCRs) streams through user feedbacks. These streams enable intelligent software evolution. Automating SCR extraction and classification is crucial with rapid growth of Mobile Apps (MA). However, significant challenges exist such as scare large-scale datasets, inconsistent classification schemes, limited data sharing and insufficient research. This study presents a first and thorough systematic survey of SCR identification from MA Reviews (MAR). In particular, we investigated how Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) enhanced identification and classification of SCR. This study has found pertinent datasets varying sizes from 5,000 to more than 18 million reviews. The key findings highlight the dominant use of Random Forest and Support Vector Machines, limited adoption of deep learning techniques, inconsistent F1-score results ranging from 0.08 to 1 and partial automation in existing SCR tools such as SURF and ChangeAdvisor. Finally, we have performed a synthesis of the studies to presents a comparative taxonomy of SCR methodologies, identify research gaps and annotation frameworks. We contend that classification schemes, shared datasets and annotation frameworks are essential for advancing SCRs and thereby improving the maintenance of mobile applications.

Software Engineering.title: VerusWeave: A Benchmark for Proof Repair in Concurrent Verus Programs
Software Engineering.summary:
Concurrent software underpins critical infrastructure, including operating systems and databases, yet thread interactions can have bugs that bypass conventional testing. Verus extends Rust with formal verification capabilities, enabling developers to specify, implement and prove the correctness of concurrent code in the same language. Although coding agents have been explored for automated proof construction, existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific examples that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols.
  To address this gap, we introduce VerusWeave, the first benchmark dedicated to concurrent proof repair, derived from four open-source projects. It comprises 75 focused tasks and 17 full-module variants that exercise features used to verify low-level concurrent code. Tasks remove selected proof annotations and require agents to fill gaps, while preserving executable code and specifications. The evaluation harness validates repairs using Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces, and resource usage. An initial evaluation of four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants, highlighting the challenge of autonomous module-wide repairs. VerusWeave provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software.

Software Engineering.title: Prompt Less, Smile More: Semantic Engineering in Lieu of Prompt Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: AI-integrated applications increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs), but their intended behavior is not always fully specified by code. Meaning Typed Programming (MTP) automates prompt construction from program structure, yet selection criteria, output requirements, and application policies can remain unstated. We introduce Semantic Engineering, a methodology for identifying such missing intent and selectively adding and refining model guidance. We realize this methodology through Semantic Context Annotations (SemTexts), a dedicated language mechanism independent of documentation and schema metadata. SemTexts associate natural-language instructions with individual program entities and use declaration scopes to determine where they apply. Our implementation extends the Jac compiler and MTP runtime to preserve these associations and select applicable guidance during automatic prompt construction. We evaluate Semantic Engineering on seven AI-integrated applications and two standard benchmarks across three models. Across the applications, it achieves a 5.46-fold reduction in integration lines of code relative to Prompt Engineering while delivering equal or better task performance in most model-application settings, reaching up to 1.83 times the task performance of Prompt Engineering.

Software Engineering.title: Claude for Excel is Transformative for Basic Spreadsheet Modeling and Analysis
Software Engineering.summary: We used the Claude Excel plug-in to build and analyze spreadsheet models for five semi structured problem statements (including a test-piece teaching case with data in multiple exhibits) and evaluated performance on modeling (what is to be coded), spreadsheet engineering (quality of coding), analysis (algorithms applied to the spreadsheet), and insight generation. Claude's ability to create a high-quality spreadsheet model from a semi structured problem statement is astoundingly excellent. Given very simple prompts, Claude generates extensive, accurate sensitivity and scenario analyses and reasonable plain English insights. Claude is Solver-aware and builds optimization models without specific prompting. Analyst productivity gains will likely be high. Business school quant courses will have to change. The way we develop human expertise will have to change.

Software Engineering.title: A Compact Formula-Aware Spreadsheet Abstraction for Large Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist spreadsheet users with tasks such as spreadsheet model construction, formula generation, and data analysis, yet their interaction with real-world spreadsheets remains limited by the mismatch between the structure of spreadsheets and the sequential textual representations typically provided to LLMs. We propose a compact formula-aware spreadsheet abstraction that represents large homogeneous ranges through their positions, types, R1C1 formula patterns, and selected boundary values. An efficient algorithm detects and structures these ranges before a textual serialization is supplied to an LLM. The abstraction is provided to the LLM before detailed spreadsheet content is submitted, improving the accuracy and efficiency of spreadsheet processing while reducing token consumption. We evaluate the method on 50 spreadsheet-query cases. The evaluation shows that the abstraction alone was sufficient to answer some queries. When additional spreadsheet content is required, the abstraction reduces the amount of data that must be submitted to the LLM, thereby reducing token consumption. The abstraction layer also improves the reliability and accuracy of spreadsheet processing. We conclude by discussing further techniques for combining spreadsheet static analysis with artificial intelligence to improve the reliability, accuracy, and efficiency of AI assisted spreadsheet tasks.

Graphics.title: SemEllipsoid: Semantic-aware Shape Abstraction with Ellipsoid
Graphics.summary: Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives - known as shape abstraction - is an actively studied problem in computer graphics with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.

Graphics.title: Frequency-Adaptive Gaussian Grids for Efficient Image Representation
Graphics.summary: Neural representation has emerged as a powerful tool to mitigate the demand for increasingly higher-resolution images. However, a fundamental trade-off remains between structured (e.g., feature grids, which offer spatial consistency) and unstructured (e.g., 2D Gaussians, which adaptively capture local variances) representations. This choice significantly affects how well an algorithm represents an image. Here, we present Gaussian-Grid, a hybrid neural representation that adaptively integrates structured and unstructured primitives. By dynamically partitioning computation between 2D Gaussian distributions and their attached multi-resolution feature grids based on the local frequency content, Gaussian-Grid automatically optimizes its architecture to match the underlying complexity of the target signal. We evaluate our approach using high-resolution natural images and demonstrate its applications as GPU-native dataset storage, showing $1.24$-$2.14\times$ decoding speed improvement and PCIe data traffic reduction of $23\times$-$176\times$ over JPEG + ZIP data archiving. The results show that Gaussian-Grid maintains small memory footprints while achieving high reconstruction fidelity across a variety of datasets.

Graphics.title: Altered Visual Hand Feedback in Virtual Reality: An Exploratory Study in Essential Tremor
Graphics.summary: Pathological tremor is the most prevalent movement disorder worldwide, characterized by involuntary muscular oscillations within a frequency of 3 to 12 Hz. Despite extensive research, the underlying mechanisms that generate and modulate tremor are not yet understood, and treatments are usually insufficient. While it is known that visual feedback is an important afferent pathway, little is known about the impact of altering the hand's visual representation on tremor expression. With the development of immersive technologies, VR poses an excellent tool to study how alterations to the representation of the hands affect tremor. In this work, we study this through two complementary experiments. In the first one, we show that a consumer-level hand-tracking system substantially attenuates tremor-band movements without preventing successful task completion. In the second one, with eight patients with essential tremor, we observe task-dependent differences in physical tremor between VR and the real world, with several patients exhibiting lower tremor-band activity in both hand kinematics and muscle oscillations, particularly during reaching tasks. Our findings represent an initial step toward validating the use of VR as an experimental tool for the research and treatment of pathological tremor, while highlighting strong user- and task-dependent effects.

Graphics.title: Toolpath Overhang Optimization for the Large-Format 3D Printing of Bespoke Shapes
Graphics.summary: This paper presents a closed curve trimming algorithm for overhang optimization in large-format support-free 3D printing of bespoke manifold shapes. Large-format 3D printing enables efficient fabrication of complex, bespoke shapes. Because of the material properties and surface quality requirements, such shapes are typically printed without support structures and have to be designed as support-free. Most current methods of overhang optimization are limited to certain types of geometry and do not apply to bespoke shapes. Our method directly optimizes sliced toolpath curves with minimal geometric modification. Given an overhang limit, it ensures that all resulting toolpath curves are strictly within the overhang limit while preserving their orientation and preventing intersections. The algorithm is based on curve offsetting and trimming, and is applicable to closed toolpath curves that represent the boundaries of a solid volume.

Graphics.title: OmniFaceRig: Fully Automatic Inner-Mouth-Aware Face Rigging Across Diverse 3D Character Topologies
Graphics.summary: Facial rigging--creating Facial Action Coding System (FACS) blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue)--remains a major bottleneck in 3D character production. We present OmniFaceRig, a fully automatic end-to-end pipeline that converts a static surface-only 3D character mesh, with no pre-modeled oral cavity, into an inner-mouth-aware FACS rig with up to 155 blendshapes, procedurally fitted teeth, gums, and tongue, and re-packed UV/texture. It supports humans, humanoids, and long- and short-muzzled animals with no manual landmarks, user-provided templates, or per-asset setup. OmniFaceRig combines a hybrid vision-language and computer vision riggability checker, a four-model face segmentation ensemble, keypoint-driven template registration, procedural inner-mouth construction, and collision-aware blendshape transfer. For non-human characters, it selects topology-specific templates with a nose-landmark-free design and uses as-rigid-as-possible deformation with signed-distance-field constraints to reduce teeth-face intersections. We also introduce Omni-Bench, an open-source benchmark of more than 1,000 biped 3D characters rigged with FACS blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry, spanning humans, humanoids, cats, dogs, and other animals. Experiments show high rigging success, nearly complete face detection recall, low inner-mouth penetration, and 20-30 s end-to-end latency per asset on a single A100 GPU.
Graphics.comment: 36 pages, 19 figures, 9 tables. Accepted to ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026). v2: revised text and appendix, updated Omni-Bench description for the public dataset release, corrected references. Project page: https://omnifacerig.github.io/ ; Dataset: https://github.com/facebookresearch/omnifacerig

Graphics.title: Piecewise CMC Segmentation for Fluidic Shaping
Graphics.summary: We present a novel mesh segmentation approach for the fabrication of 3D geometries using fluidic shaping. The physics of fluidic shaping gives rise to Constant Mean Curvature (CMC) surfaces due to interfacial tension between the polymer fluid used to shape the 3D structure and an immersion fluid of equal density. Our mesh segmentation algorithm partitions the mesh into a piecewise CMC surface, such that every segment is a CMC approximation to the target within a user specified tolerance. We run a CMC evolution procedure in the loop during segmentation to find physically stable CMC surfaces that can be reliably fabricated. We extract a wireframe scaffold from the seams of this segmentation and inject polymer fluid into the frame for curing. The structure cures as a single, continuous, isotropic volume, yielding nanometer scale roughness on the interior surface of each segment without the costly post-processing or smoothing that conventional state-of-the-art approaches require for comparable surface quality.

Graphics.title: How to Simplify a Line Chart: A Taxonomy and Feature-Based Evaluation
Graphics.summary: Simplifying large or noisy time-series is often a prerequisite for producing interpretable line charts, yet existing methods vary widely in how they alter visual features such as trends, extrema, periodicity, curvature, roughness, and overall complexity. We introduce a feature-based taxonomy of line chart simplification that evaluates 19 commonly used algorithms across three families: Transformers, Reducers, and Aggregators. We also formalize 12 perceptually motivated, computationally defined visual features commonly used when analyzing time-series in line charts. We assess preservation using multiple similarity metrics per feature to capture different aspects of fidelity, yielding 21 distinct feature-preservation measurements. To capture the trade-off between fidelity and simplicity, we introduce a Feature--Complexity (FC) score that combines feature preservation with complexity. Our systematic evaluation on 80 datasets reveals distinct family-level patterns: Transformers such as Gaussian, Mean, and Median filters achieve A-mode grades on nearly all metrics but retain full temporal resolution; Reducers such as Douglas-Peucker and M4 receive predominantly D-F mode grades trading fidelity for a reduction in the number of rendered points; and Aggregators ASAP and PAA occupy a middle ground with primarily B-C mode grades. We further characterize the predictability of algorithm behavior across datasets: some methods produce consistent grades regardless of dataset type (Gaussian, Mean, Douglas-Peucker), while others exhibit high data-dependency, with performance varying substantially based on dataset characteristics (FPCS, ASAP). An interactive website supporting exploration of all evaluated techniques, datasets, and results is available at https://feature-taxonomy.vercel.app/.

Computation and Language.title: Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models
Computation and Language.summary: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.
Computation and Language.comment: Published as conference proceeding for NeurIPS 2026. Last two authors advised equally

Computation and Language.title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
Computation and Language.summary: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.

Computation and Language.title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
Computation and Language.summary: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19--23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running $24.5\times$ faster on TREC DL and $16.7\times$ faster on BRIGHT.

Computation and Language.title: Tracing the Influence of Retrieved Literature on Scientific Ideation in LLMs
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate research ideas from scientific literature. Existing systems combine literature retrieval with search, generation, and refinement, making it difficult to determine how the retrieval strategy itself shapes the ideas generated. We isolate this contribution by comparing five retrieval strategies and a No Literature baseline under a shared generation protocol, using 45,000 ideas across 15 machine learning topics and ten open-weight models. Relative to no literature basline, all five retrieval strategies reduce diversity among ideas generated from the same set of papers by $5.6\%$--$17.9\%$, while most increase diversity by $10.2\%$--$18.1\%$ when ideas from different sets are pooled. Effects on idea quality and novelty are modest on average but vary across topics. We further apply a JSD-based attribution method to trace the influence of individual input papers on each idea's motivation, core idea, approach, and validation. In $79.3\%$ of ideas, only one or two distinct papers receive the highest attribution scores across these four parts. These leading sources often recur across ideas generated from the same set of papers, and groups with more varied source attribution contain more diverse ideas ($r=0.70$). These findings motivate various sets of literature and the use of attribution to guide the choice of sources for subsequent ideas.

Computation and Language.title: Metacognitive Decoding: Efficient Inference for Diffusion Language Agents
Computation and Language.summary: Diffusion language models offer a promising path to efficient agents through parallel token generation. However, efficient interaction requires adapting both where computation is spent and how much text is generated. We introduce a metacognitive controller that guides diffusion generation according to the needs of the current response and the agent's interaction with the environment. It learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should extend, reducing overall computation within responses. Our controller, a lightweight plug-in for the diffusion backbone, is trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness and generation cost. This approach connects the agent's generation process to the interaction the agent serves. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that our approach reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average compared with the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our approach.

Computation and Language.title: TamilEOT: A Dataset and Model for Semantic End-of-Turn Detection in Tamil Telephone Speech
Computation and Language.summary: A voice agent must decide, at each pause, whether the speaker has finished or is still thinking. Without a model of the language, systems fall back to a fixed silence timeout: too short, and the agent interrupts; too long, and every turn pays the full wait. We release TamilEOT, to our knowledge the first open dataset and detector for semantic end-of-turn detection in a South Indian language: 18,485 labelled turn boundaries from 116 real Tamil telephone conversations, two audio-only detectors built on Smart Turn v3's architecture, and a turn-level companion set of 4,774 whole turns with their pause structure. On a held-out split of 4,168 clips from 30 unseen calls, accuracy rises from 70.30% zero-shot to 83.71% (8.7 MB) and 86.13% (21 MB); ROC-AUC rises from 0.751 to 0.921. Both run in under 150 ms single-threaded on a laptop CPU. We also report what building it cost. Our rule-derived negative-class labels scored 44.4% against a blind human pass, below chance, because the rule answered a different question than the model is asked; an audio-LLM labeller at 97.5% agreement replaced them for US$5.69. Of six training levers, only encoder capacity moved the result: three identical runs spanned 0.87 accuracy points, the floor below which nothing else here is a finding. Replaying labelled boundaries through the production VAD and streaming adapter costs a further 2.60 points, and 7.8% of boundaries never reach the model at all. Data, weights, code and every negative result are public.
Computation and Language.comment: 14 pages, 7 tables. Code, data and models: https://github.com/santhosh-005/tamil-eot

Computation and Language.title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
Computation and Language.summary: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

Computation and Language.title: Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context
Computation and Language.summary:
Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP) draft head, assumed to be cheap beside verification. A shipped full-attention MTP head can become disproportionately expensive beside a hybrid target at long context. The head attends over the full KV cache for each of $γ$ draft forwards per decode step, while only 9-25% of target layers retain full attention, so a single draft layer can issue context reads at a rate comparable to the whole target. On hard, low-acceptance workloads, deep native MTP becomes net-negative: slower than no speculation.
  We apply a StreamingLLM-style window plus attention sink to the draft only (Windowed-MTP); target verification remains full-context, so the target distribution is preserved. The intervention is training-free and drop-in. On three models from two hybrid families (Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2) at 1M context on one GPU in SGLang, it provides an acceptance-free 1.28-1.44x per-decode-step speedup over native MTP. The speedup grows with context; at matched acceptance, TPOT improves by the same factor. The window removes most of the draft's working set, and a compact ring buffer converts that reduction into physical capacity: it reclaims the otherwise dead draft pool, a measured 7.7-11.1% of total KV at 1M, making room for one additional concurrent 1M request in the Qwen-35B batch sweep.
Computation and Language.comment: 29 pages, 5 figures, 16 tables. v2: Windowed draft attention is merged upstream in SGLang (PR #32673). Code: https://github.com/avalliappan-nvidia/windowed-mtp-b200

Computation and Language.title: RangeSWA: Training-Free Length Extrapolation for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.

Computation and Language.title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
Computation and Language.summary: Prior research into interpretability does not test whether a representation stays consistent under paraphrasing. Each pair of paraphrases can be thought of as a local witness that two activations should be the same. From these local witnesses we can build a cellular sheaf on the paraphrase graph. The question of what is consistent under paraphrasing can be answered by the Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ given a frozen model. No training required. Our kernel $H^0$ gives us a content subspace. We show that with only 20 dims the kernel outperforms the subspace that LEACE retains with all dims on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval by $+17.1$\,pp on average across 8 models. By constraining all paraphrases of a fact together we see an additional increase of $+6.5$\,pp. Our spectral complement shows us where the causal influence is concentrated. Ablating the coordinates that vary the most when paraphrased (which approximates ablating the spectral complement at the coordinate level) leads to $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ larger changes in model outputs compared to ablating coordinates with matched per-coordinate variability. We find this across 9 models from 124M to 13B params. By stacking layers we can create a grid which has $b_1 = N(L-1)$ algebraic 1-cycles. The harmonic mass derived from the model varies by nearly 3 orders of magnitude between the 6 architectures. It also tracks the order of steering fragility (Spearman's $ρ= 0.90$, exact one-sided permutation $p = 0.014$). The kernel, its spectral complement and the harmonic mass all come from the same paraphrase graph. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/gluing-lc-page/.
Computation and Language.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Poster, ICLR Unifying Concept Representation Learning

Computation and Language.title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results
Computation and Language.summary: AI answers require more than apparent correctness: reviewers need to inspect their recorded basis. We introduce the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation. We reference KLM v0.3 (repository tag v0.3.0). Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author-reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work.
Computation and Language.comment: 47 pages, 1 figure, 14 tables. Includes Appendix A

Computation and Language.title: PersonaChatBench: Evaluating Chat Assistants with Diverse Simulated Users
Computation and Language.summary: Conversational assistants are expected to help people with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and communication styles. Yet evaluations centered on a single cooperative user provide limited insight into how reliably an assistant serves users with different personas. We introduce PersonaChatBench, a framework for evaluating task competence and responsiveness to diverse user needs. PersonaChatBench pairs the same underlying task with multiple simulated users, each guided by a private persona card that specifies distinct needs, preferences, and interaction behaviors. By holding the task fixed while varying the user, the framework examines how assistant performance changes across user conditions. We evaluate 20 language models across six domains, separately assessing native task outcomes, fulfillment of expressed persona needs, and simulator fidelity. Our results show that task performance and need fulfillment vary across personas and domains. Strong task performance does not necessarily translate into satisfying individual needs, and models' relative strengths in meeting those needs are not consistent across domains. PersonaChatBench makes these differences measurable, revealing gaps obscured by aggregate scores and helping identify which users an assistant serves well and where adaptation is needed. It provides a basis for evaluating consistency across users and guiding the development of assistants that better accommodate diverse needs in everyday applications.

Computation and Language.title: Robustness of Chatbot LLM Judgments of Presidential Actions and Hypothetical Reforms
Computation and Language.summary: Chatbots are increasingly consulted about public affairs, and their judgments of policies are useful only if they are robust. We measure this robustness in the setting of an ordinary user, through consumer chat interfaces. For 30 days, five chatbot configurations (Mistral, Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Opus at two effort settings) were asked twice a day to score the long-term effect on the United States of 40 actions of the last four presidential administrations and of 15 hypothetical reforms, each with a confidence and a short comment. The judgments are robust: all configurations agree on the sign and the ranking of the administrations' mean scores, and two different configurations asked on the same day give opposite signs to the same action in about 4% of cases. Responses from different days differ more than same-day responses (which shared the order of the items); the difference grows slowly over the month, except where the service itself changed. We identify three such changes, which shifted the judgments while leaving little or no trace in the interface. Treating the comments as a retrieval task, we find them specific to each item and consistent across runs and chatbots, with lexical and embedding similarities agreeing. We release the dataset of 16,500 judgments.

Computation and Language.title: CRoS: Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs Improves Accuracy and Reasoning Faithfulness
Computation and Language.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the standard method for training language models to reason. However, RLVR typically relies solely on outcome correctness, which does not guarantee that the CoT causally contributes to the final answer. Without this connection, outcome rewards may fail to reinforce high-quality reasoning. Existing causality metrics assess CoT causality by perturbing the CoT, such as deleting reasoning steps or injecting errors, and measuring changes in the final answer. However, these perturbations inevitably alter information in each step. Consequently, high causality scores may reflect sensitivity to information changes introduced by perturbation rather than true causality. Such confounding effects further induce undesirable reasoning behaviors when these metrics are used as training rewards, including generating less informative CoTs and reducing exploration and self-correction. To address this problem, we propose CRoS (Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs), a novel CoT causality metric that perturbs the order of reasoning steps without altering content, thereby preserving information within each step. On Reasoning Gym with Gemma-3-4B, CRoS outperforms existing causality and outcome rewards in out-of-domain accuracy, CoT quality, and CoT faithfulness. Specifically, CRoS achieves 46.8% accuracy on five unseen logic and games datasets, outperforming the strongest baseline (43.8%). It also achieves better CoT quality, consistently outperforming baselines in CoT-Pass@K from K=1 to 128, averaging 43.4% vs. 41.4%. For CoT faithfulness, CRoS achieves a hint acknowledgment score of 34.0% vs. 20.2%.
Computation and Language.comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 14 tables. Project page: https://xxiaoyuuuu.github.io/CRoS-Page

Computation and Language.title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
Computation and Language.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

Computation and Language.title: Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To
Computation and Language.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly ship with explicit "thinking modes", yet their counterpart, "no-thinking", has received far less attention. We study LLMs' no-thinking behavior along two axes. a. How to measure no-thinking? Prior work typically defines no-thinking through proxies such as a disabled thinking mode or the absence of long traces. These proxies are unreliable: disabled thinking modes may still emit reasoning, while long traces may contain filler rather than genuine inference. We instead normalize each response into a pre-answer trace and final answer, and evaluate it at three levels: (i) Empty-Thinking Rate for strict answer-only compliance; (ii) instruction-aware Question-Pre-answer Relevance for similarity between the question and pre-answer trace; and (iii) LLM-as-judge Explicit Inference Rate for visible explicit inference. Together, these metrics distinguish answer-only output, relevant but non-inferential text, and explicit inference. b. How does no-thinking vary across tasks and models? We evaluate six prompting interventions on six LLMs across Boolean, multiple-choice, and open-ended questions. We find that explicit no-think controls cannot reliably eliminate visible inference. Models instead exhibit "Thinking Inertia": explicit inference persists even under strict controls and becomes more prevalent as the answer space opens. Accuracy remains stable on Boolean and multiple-choice tasks, whereas open-ended tasks reveal a trade-off between answer-only compliance and task accuracy. Rewriting the same questions across answer spaces shows that supplying candidate answers makes answer-only responses easier to produce. These findings establish no-thinking as a non-trivial capability: stopping explicit reasoning cannot be assumed from model settings or instructions alone and deserves systematic evaluation alongside reasoning ability.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026. Website: https://thinking-inertia.github.io GitHub: https://github.com/thinking-inertia/code

Computation and Language.title: Asynchronous Flow Map Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.

Computation and Language.title: Imputation of Public Opinion Data with Large Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely evaluated as simulators of survey responses, yet applied survey research mostly faces item nonresponse. Imputation fills in those missing values to restore the overall structure of a partially observed dataset and has its own well-defined evaluation criteria, which differ fundamentally from prediction accuracy. We present the first evaluation of LLM imputation against proper multiple-imputation metrics and statistical baselines on more than 5 million imputed responses from four public opinion surveys under various missingness mechanisms. We evaluate in-context learning (ICL) for this task by investigating 84 ICL configurations and comparing the best-performing configurations on six open-weight LLMs. The strongest ICL approach improves on zero-shot persona prompting but remains, at best, competitive with statistical baselines (MICE PMM, TabPFN). ICL approaches are sensitive to survey topics and consume 2-3 orders of magnitude more compute. Moreover, prediction metrics commonly used in LLM survey simulation (macro-F1, TVD) do not reliably track imputation quality. Our findings highlight the importance of fit-for-purpose evaluation for LLM imputation, where established multiple imputation remains the better default.

Computation and Language.title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
Computation and Language.summary: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

Computation and Language.title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting
Computation and Language.summary: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.
Computation and Language.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/SeverinVisionary/prior-shift-diagnostic

Computation and Language.title: Exploring the potential and limitations of Model Merging for Multi-Domain Adaptation in ASR
Computation and Language.summary: Model merging is a scalable alternative to multi-task training that combines the capabilities of multiple specialised models into a single model. This is particularly attractive for large speech foundation models, which are typically adapted through domain-specific fine-tuning, resulting in multiple customised checkpoints, for which repeating full fine-tuning when new data becomes available is computationally prohibitive. In this work, we study model merging for multi-domain ASR and benchmark 11 merging algorithms for 10 European Portuguese domains, evaluating in-domain accuracy, robustness under distribution shift, as well as English and multilingual performance. We further propose BoostedTSV-M, a new merging algorithm based on TSV-M that mitigates rank collapse via singular-value boosting and improves numerical stability. Overall, our approach outperforms full fine-tuning on European Portuguese while preserving out-of-distribution generalisation in a single model.

Computation and Language.title: DAMI: Dual-Axis Memory Initialization for Enhanced Long-Context Retrieval in Gated Linear Attention
Computation and Language.summary: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.

Computation and Language.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

Computation and Language.title: Beyond Public Access in LLM Pre-Training Data
Computation and Language.summary: Using a legally obtained dataset of 34 copyrighted O'Reilly Media books (13,962 paragraphs), we apply the DE-COP membership inference attack to test whether OpenAI models show recognition of non-public (pay-walled) content they were not licensed to train on. Our main contribution is examining non-public books, which allows us to consider potential access violations and not just training inclusion. Our results suggest that GPT-4o, OpenAI's more recent and capable model in our sample, exhibits patterns consistent with recognition of non-public books, with an AUROC score of 0.82 (95% bootstrapped CI: 0.60-0.96) -- where above 50% is better than random chance. GPT-3.5 Turbo (trained two years prior) and the smaller GPT-4o Mini both score near chance recognition on non-public data (0.54 and 0.56, respectively). Results are robust to independent paraphrasers (Gemma and Qwen) and leave-one-book-out sensitivity analyses. We also test both GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini, with the same October 2023 training cutoff date, to ensure the model is not simply identifying language shifts over time. These findings support disclosure requirements for pre-training data provenance and formal licensing markets for training content. Results remain preliminary given the small book sample, possible contamination of post-cutoff controls, and differences across models in size, architecture, and training composition.
Computation and Language.comment: 38 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables. Updated to reflect the published version in AI and Ethics

Computation and Language.title: Optimal Multi-bit Generative Watermarking Schemes Under Worst-Case False-Alarm Constraints
Computation and Language.summary: This paper considers the problem of multi-bit generative watermarking for large language models under a worst-case false-alarm constraint. Prior work established a lower bound on the achievable miss-detection probability in the finite-token regime and proposed a scheme claimed to achieve this bound. We show, however, that the proposed scheme is in fact suboptimal. We then develop two new encoding-decoding constructions that attain the previously established lower bound, thereby completely characterizing the optimal multi-bit watermarking performance. Our approach formulates the watermark design problem as a linear program and derives the structural conditions under which optimality can be achieved. In addition, we identify the failure mechanism of the previous construction and compare the tradeoffs between the two proposed schemes.

Computation and Language.title: Instrument-Anchored LLM Judges Transfer Expert Counseling-Quality Ratings Across Three German Corpora
Computation and Language.summary: Automatic assessment of communication quality in counseling conversations is bottlenecked by data: expert-rated corpora are small and expensive to grow. Therefore we study cross-domain prediction of the expert's overall impression across three German simulated-counseling corpora from one university (two general-practice medical, one parent-teacher; $n=195$ sessions). Features are construct scores that four small LLM judges assign from the transcript, drawn from the experts' own rating instruments, plus a compact nonverbal block; all models are open-weight and run locally, preserving data protection. Trained on the other two corpora, this stack predicts the held-out corpus at Spearman $ρ= .533$; in-domain training on the same sessions falls about a fifth short ($.420$; paired gap $+.113$, 95% CI $[+.067, +.157]$), and the gap holds at matched training size and on identical test sessions. The signal lies in what is said: the four judges alone transfer at $.523$, and the nonverbal block adds $+.01$ (CI includes zero). Asking a judge for instrument constructs instead of generic dialogue qualities raises its transfer by about 30% ($.32$ to $.42$); restoring speaker attribution where per-speaker audio was lost is worth $+.08$ to $+.10$ on that fold. Where a program's own ratings are scarce, other programs' data is a viable training set and language carries it.

Computation and Language.title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
Computation and Language.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks.
