Systems and Control.summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a standard way to keep a planner inside a safe set, but they assume control affine dynamics, a barrier function given in closed form, and a known nominal controller. Integral control barrier functions (ICBFs) remove the first assumption and absorb input constraints, yet they still assume a given nominal controller and a barrier function. In this work, we present an approach to learn all three from data, using neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the dynamics, imitation for the nominal controller, and supervised regression for the barrier function. The learned dynamics, nominal controller, and the barrier function are used to build the ICBF filter constraint analytically. Furthermore, the barrier is trained on viability rather than geometry, meaning that a state counts as safe only if some emergency maneuver can still avoid the constraint under the actuator limits, a correction that geometric labels miss entirely and that grows with speed. Actuator limits then enter the online program as hard bounds while the learned barrier rows may be relaxed, which keeps the program solvable at every state and the actuator limits exact, and we bound how far the input it returns can drift from the one the true models would give. On agile racing with a 6-D dynamic bicycle, the filter removes all 12 unsafe episodes from 200 held out layouts at an unchanged success rate and above 100 Hz on one CPU core, holds the input constraint on every episode of a benchmark where a jointly trained baseline holds it on 53.38%, and keeps that advantage under large errors in the plant friction.

Systems and Control.title: MERIS: Adaptive Real-Time Scheduling of Refined Inference DAGs in Dynamic Robotic Environments
Systems and Control.summary: Robots deployed in dynamic environments execute changing directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workloads under limited compute and timing budgets. This article presents MERIS, a framework for model scheduling under real-time constraints that combines proportional intermediate deadlines, MIMONet-aware graph refinement, and event-driven synchronization for multi-task inference on resource-constrained robotic platforms. We distinguish three representations: the application DAG, each MIMONet's internal encoder/decoder graph, and the refined scheduling DAG, and make the scope of the timing argument explicit. If the profiled execution bounds, release assumptions, precedence barriers, and per-level capacity premises hold, satisfaction of the assigned sub-deadlines composes to the end-to-end deadline. For non-partitionable tasks, we define a profile-bounded admission rule; before interpreting that rule as empirical timing evidence, we require direct per-task completion checks. We report run-level QoE alongside the offered-node deadline missing rate, making explicit that run completion and successful service of every node are different outcomes. We propose a comprehensive minibenchmark for evaluating the performance of schedulers under various DNN-driven autonomous driving scenarios. Extensive experiments on Nano Orin, AGX Orin, and M3 Max demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

Systems and Control.title: How to Peel with a Knife: Aligning Fine-Grained Manipulation with Human Preference
Systems and Control.summary: Many essential manipulation tasks - such as food preparation, surgery, and craftsmanship - remain difficult for autonomous robots. These tasks are characterized not only by contact-rich, force-sensitive dynamics, but also by their "implicit" success criteria: unlike pick-and-place, task quality in these domains is continuous and subjective (e.g. how well a potato is peeled), making quantitative evaluation and reward design difficult. We present a learning framework for such tasks, using peeling with a knife as a representative example. Our approach follows a two-stage pipeline: first, we learn a robust initial policy via force-aware data collection and imitation learning, enabling generalization across object variations; second, we refine the policy through preference-based finetuning using a learned reward model that combines quantitative task metrics with qualitative human feedback, aligning policy behavior with human-evaluated task quality. Using only 50~200 peeling trajectories, our system achieves 100% same-produce success on cucumbers, apples, and potatoes, with performance improving by up to 40% through preference-based finetuning. Remarkably, policies trained on one produce category also transfer zero-shot to selected held-out produce categories, achieving 50% success on zucchini, 90% on pear, and 80% on daikon radish.
Systems and Control.comment: Project page can be found at https://toruowo.github.io/peel

Systems and Control.title: Coupling Europe's Capacity Markets
Systems and Control.summary: European Member States are increasingly introducing national capacity mechanisms (CMs) to manage growing adequacy risks. However, isolated national CMs are inefficient in highly interconnected electricity systems, such as the European system. While progress has been made in facilitating cross-border participation by generation capacity in CMs, existing arrangements are prone to under- or over-investment and do not properly value the contribution of interconnection capacity to Member States' adequacy targets. We argue that national capacity markets, offering long-term contracts, need a second tier: an annual capacity auction coupled across zones, which sets zonal prices for firm, deliverable capacity. We design such an auction by extending the logic of flow-based market coupling to capacity markets. In a comparative analysis of different market design scenarios in an illustrative multi-zone case study, using a bespoke long-run equilibrium problem, we show that the proposed auction removes the circular dependency between imports and available capacity in current cross-border participation schemes, locates investment where it is cheapest while keeping it deliverable under network constraints in defined scarcity situations, and makes the value of additional interconnection capacity explicit.

Systems and Control.title: Unbeatable imitation of a friend
Systems and Control.summary: Imitation sometimes achieves success in multi-agent situations even though it is very simple. In repeated games, success of imitation has been characterized by unbeatability against other agents. Previous studies specified conditions under which imitation is unbeatable against co-players in repeated symmetric games, and clarified that the existence of unbeatable imitation is strongly related to the existence of payoff-controlling strategies, called zero-determinant strategies. However, these results were on the situations in which one repeated game is played by one group of players. It was pointed out that imitation of other players in the same group and imitation of other players in the same role in other groups generally result in different outcomes. Here, we investigate the existence condition of unbeatable imitation in the latter situations, described by two concurrent repeated games played by two different groups of players. We find that the existence condition of unbeatable imitation is stronger than the existence condition of unbeatable zero-determinant strategies, whereas both are very limited. Furthermore, we find that adding exploration can make an imitation strategy unbeatable even in games where imitation without exploration can be beaten. Our findings suggest a strong relation between unbeatable imitation and payoff control even in the two concurrent repeated game situations.

Systems and Control.title: Central pivot point control of a body-attached spring-mass runner: periodic gaits, stabilization, template embedding and approximate analytic return maps
Systems and Control.summary: The spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) describes the center-of-mass (COM) motion of runners but has no trunk. In trunk models, the hip torque couples posture and COM motion and destroys the central-force structure on which SLIP analysis relies. As a result, trunk models have been studied almost only numerically. We show that this structure can be restored. The central pivot point (CPP), a hip-torque law that directs the ground reaction force through the COM, decouples pitch exactly and reduces stance to a planar central-force problem. At upright posture, time-reversal symmetry produces one-parameter families of periodic gaits. A stance-phase pitch law and a stride-level regulator stabilize all computed gaits, also with bounded hip torque and friction. Under CPP, any radial force law in virtual-leg coordinates can be embedded independently of posture. For a linear radial template, the stance radius and the constant-momentum sweep have exact closed forms. With a new gravity correction, the resulting analytic return map, to our knowledge the first for a trunk model, predicts liftoff velocity and apex position with mean errors of 1.6% and 0.9%. The natural gaits of the embedded runner are symmetric and need no force step at touchdown. A near-reversibility argument explains their unit multiplier, and a scalar equation predicts them within 0.8%. A deadbeat stride controller based on the analytic map tracks changes of speed, height and posture. CPP thus makes trunk models accessible to the analytic tools developed for SLIP.
Systems and Control.comment: 21 pages, 15 figures. Submitted to Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science

Systems and Control.title: Convex Reformulation of Minkowski-Sum Outer Approximation for Matrix Ellipsoids in Data-Driven Control
Systems and Control.summary: Approximating Minkowski sums of matrix ellipsoids by a single matrix ellipsoid provides a tractable description of noise bounds for controller design from noisy data. Existing linear matrix inequality (LMI) conditions can be used to compute such approximations, but directly solving the resulting optimization problems can be computationally expensive. This paper develops an efficient method for finding a minimum-volume outer matrix ellipsoid under these LMI conditions. Although the corresponding problem for ordinary vector-valued ellipsoids is convex, the objective function in the matrix-valued case is nonconvex. We find that the problem admits an equivalent convex reformulation, which resolves this difficulty. We first eliminate the matrix variables using equivalent LMI transformations and objective monotonicity, leaving one positive scalar variable per matrix ellipsoid in the sum. We then show that the objective becomes convex after a logarithmic change of variables. The resulting problem contains neither LMI constraints nor matrix variables and can therefore be solved efficiently. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed method is substantially faster than the LMI-based method. An application to data-driven control further illustrates the tradeoff between guaranteed control performance and computation time.

Systems and Control.title: Winding the Field, Not the Wire: Overlaying Magnetics to Improve Current Dynamics in Modular Power Electronics
Systems and Control.summary:
Modular power electronics scale power capacity by distributing it across cascaded modules.
  State-of-the-art modular multilevel converters further introduce dynamic inter-module switched-capacitor exchange and balancing through parallelization.
  In larger converters, however, this mode needs inter-module inductance to control the equilibration currents.
  Specifically, differential-mode inductance limits these currents, but existing solutions require conductor re-routing and introduce parasitic resistance.
  This work presents a non-intrusive resistance-free differential-mode inductance solution: a figure-of-eight-shaped magnetic core that guides the magnetic flux path around existing conductors, such as high-current bus bars.
  This design adds differential-mode inductance without modifying the conductors.
  We fabricated a core that provides a 1.52 uH differential-mode inductance while suppressing the common-mode inductance to only 7% of the DM inductance.
  The core reduces the inter-module current surge from 20.46 A to 7.76 A. The original conductors remain intact.

Systems and Control.title: Touching Projected Agents through the DAT Screen -System Design and Questions of Interaction Boundaries-
Systems and Control.summary: Touching a virtual agent involves more than detecting a finger on a display: the contact surface can deform and resist the user's push, and the agent can respond to that action. We describe the Desktop Amid Touch (DAT) screen, which combines spatial projection onto a semi-transparent, deformable mesh with touch sensing and motorized control of resistance to indentation. An initial prototype detected a single touch and estimated its position and depth from tension changes around a flexible projection screen. A subsequent prototype added motorized tension control to vary the screen's resistance to indentation. We describe the tension-controlled DAT implementation and its demonstrations, distinguishing what has been observed from what remains an open design question. These capabilities raise a design question: should touchable virtual agents respond as though they had preferences or boundaries, and under what conditions should such behavior be implemented on systems like DAT. The present paper describes a system and frames this question; it does not establish how users interpret an agent's refusal or consent.
Systems and Control.comment: The 2nd International Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies (TBSA_2nd) in conjunction with HAI 2026, 4 pages, 4 figures

Systems and Control.title: Differentially Private Consensus for Time-Delay Multi-agent Systems
Systems and Control.summary: This paper is concerned with the differentially private consensus problem for discrete-time multi-agent systems with communication delays. The purpose of the paper is to achieve differentially private consensus for such systems while protecting the entire delayed initial histories of all agents. A novel adjacency relation for delayed histories is introduced, and a Laplace-noise-based privacy mechanism is developed, where the noise variance is allowed to vary with time and even increase. By using the difference resolvent function method, decay estimates for the fundamental solutions of the delayed difference equations are derived. Based on these estimates and a backstepping technique, mean square weak consensus, mean square strong consensus, and almost sure strong consensus are established. The estimates for the fundamental solutions are also used to derive an explicit sensitivity bound. Furthermore, a constructive parameter design is provided to achieve a prescribed infinite-horizon $ε^\star$-differential privacy level. Numerical simulations illustrate the theoretical results.

Systems and Control.title: SPIRAL-PO: Symbolic Identification of Partially Observed Nonlinear Dynamics with Application to Rotating Machinery
Systems and Control.summary: Many engineering systems contain states that cannot be measured directly, yet these hidden states act on the measured outputs. We present SPIRAL-PO (Symbolic Physics-Informed Residual Augmentation Loop - Partially Observed), a framework for identifying an interpretable observable-space closure: a model, written in the measured coordinates, of how the unmeasured states act on the measured dynamics. A physics seed is augmented by candidate terms from a mechanism-labeled library; terms are selected by statistical tests designed for numerically differentiated, serially correlated data, using a weak (integral) formulation, and are checked on independent records. For an idealized regression we give sufficient conditions for recovering the closure coefficients, a rank condition under which no estimator can recover them, and a per-term detection bound; these results apply only to systems that admit an instantaneous observable closure. On a simulated four-degree-of-freedom vertical rotor with cubic bearing stiffness, in which only the lateral displacements are measured, the method recovers the gyroscopic and cubic-stiffness signatures of the hidden tilt dynamics in every noise realization at 2% noise; with a mechanism removed it never admits the cubic term and admits the gyroscopic term in 15-25% of realizations, above the nominal level, because the closure is only partly instantaneous. A residual network and a quasi-random projection stage add no measurable benefit, and pointwise tests that ignore the serial correlation of differentiated data admit absent mechanisms more often. On a laboratory rotor with simultaneous x,y measurement and an order-tracked speed, the method detects only a speed-dependent stiffening; gyroscopic and cubic terms obtained with an assumed constant-deceleration speed are consistent with the speed error, which produces such terms in simulation.
Systems and Control.comment: Revised version, under review at Nonlinear Dynamics. 32 pages, 6 figures, 14 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23705395

Systems and Control.title: SEAMLiS: Visibility-Aware Safety for Perception-Limited Multi-Robot Exploration
Systems and Control.summary: Autonomous exploration in unknown environments is typically driven by informative frontiers, viewpoints, or trajectories, while local safety controllers avoid obstacles represented in the current map. Under finite sensing range and limited field of view, this separation can be unsafe: an exploration stack may plan optimistically through unobserved space and steer the sensor toward information gain rather than along the direction of motion, causing hidden obstacles to be detected too late for bounded-actuation avoidance. This paper presents SEAMLiS (Safe Exploration for Autonomous Multi-Robot Systems Under Limited Sensing), a modular execution-layer safety framework for decentralized multi-robot exploration. SEAMLiS preserves the upstream exploration stack, including the goal allocator and local planner, and enforces safety at the execution layer through perception-aware attitude and positional filters. A gatekeeper-based attitude filter switches between a visibility-promoting yaw policy and a velocity-tracking backup policy to preserve visibility of the critical known-free/unknown boundary with sufficient braking margin. A Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based positional filter then avoids known obstacles, newly detected obstacles, and other robots. We provide sufficient collision-avoidance conditions and validate the framework in randomized simulation, Isaac Sim, and Crazyflie hardware experiments. Results show collision-free exploration across tested single- and multi-robot settings while retaining much of the efficiency of visibility-promoting yaw control.

Systems and Control.title: Finding optimal measurement sequences for broken or constrained measuring devices
Systems and Control.summary: Measuring devices do not always function perfectly due to fatigue, damage, or malfunction. When device repair or replacement is not possible, it becomes necessary to seek optimal measurements from a broken device. We show this is possible via a sequential decision making process where we optimize measurement sequences over the remaining available measurements using information theory. With dynamic programming, we show greedy measurement sequences are always suboptimal for a simple class of measurement constraints. Greedy measurement sequences generally lead to equiprobable measurement outcomes, while the optimal policy is found to select each measurement in such a way as to assign a low probability to any measurement outcome that triggers a constraint condition; leading to measurement outcomes that are not equiprobable. A measurement sequence generated under this policy is shown to decompress its source: that is, the expected number of measurement outcomes is strictly greater than the number of bits it encodes, defining a key property of constrained measurements. Dynamic programming is inefficient for finding optimal measurement sequences, so we develop an alternative algorithm related to optimal binary decision trees. By deriving upper and lower complexity bounds for the task, we propose this algorithm as an efficient means to find optimal measurements for a broken or constrained measuring device.

Systems and Control.title: Beyond Binary Controllability: Reachability Margins for Power Systems via Scalable Screening
Systems and Control.summary: This paper studies unreachability screening for power systems, focusing on the inadequate control authority that arises under stressed grid conditions. Its main result is an infeasibility \textit{margin} for linearized differential algebraic equation models that quantifies how far a prescribed terminal target lies from the reachable set in finite time. The paper specifically develops a conic benchmark method together with two first order methods based on projected subgradients and bundle updates for scalably repeated screening. Studies on IEEE benchmark networks show reduced terminal reachability under stressed conditions and tighter actuation limits, while first order methods remain accurate and substantially faster on large systems. Comparisons with standard reachability methods such as CORA further demonstrate the usefulness and scalability of the proposed infeasibility margins. All results and codes are included in a Github repository.

Systems and Control.title: Weak and Strong Data Informativity with Structural Priors for System Analysis
Systems and Control.summary: When measurement data are insufficient for unique system identification, data informativity evaluates whether a dataset determines a property across all systems consistent with the data. This paper introduces a unified framework distinguishing between weak and strong data informativity under prior structural knowledge described by affine constraints: data are weakly informative if at least one system consistent with the data and prior knowledge possesses the target property, and strongly informative if every consistent system satisfies it. The latter is consistent with the notion of data informativity in the existing literature. By explicitly parameterizing all consistent systems as affine functions of free parameters via the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, we characterize these notions for fundamental system properties-including controllability, stabilizability, and stability. This formulation establishes that verifying weak and strong informativity, when tractable, reduces to rank tests of matrix pencils constructed from the data and prior knowledge. Our findings show that structural priors can lower data-excitation requirements and enable reliable analysis even when data fail to be strongly informative. Finally, the framework is extended to a class of noisy data.

Systems and Control.title: When Can Phasor-Domain Device Models Be Trusted for Electromechanical Stability Analysis of Grid-Forming Converter-Dominated Microgrids?
Systems and Control.summary: Grid-forming (GFM) converter-dominated microgrids are often analyzed using reduced-order phasor-domain electromechanical GFM models, but the validity of these models is often taken for granted. Assuming ideal inner-loop tracking (IILT) of terminal-voltage references, these models neglect the inner-loop and filter dynamics at the electromagnetic-transient (EMT) timescale to simplify stability analysis. This paper argues that such neglected dynamics can destabilize the system, invalidating the stability conclusions drawn from the IILT model. To address this cross-timescale stability issue, we formulate the validity of the IILT stability conclusion as a robust-stability certification problem. The EMT-induced model mismatch between the reduced-order converter model and the actual converter model is represented as a structured uncertainty embedded around the IILT feedback loop. This yields a frequency-resolved interaction index and a structured singular-value sufficient certificate for determining when the stability conclusion of the IILT model can be certified with respect to a prescribed EMT uncertainty weight. The uncertainty weight can be obtained from detailed EMT models or terminal reference-response measurements. Case studies confirm that the proposed certificate correctly certifies model validity and identifies the loss of trustworthiness. We also demonstrate that the measurement-based uncertainty weights closely match the model-based ones, which enables deployment without accessing inner-loop models.

Systems and Control.title: Valuing Static Synchronous Series Compensators in the U.S. Grid: Planning with Transmission Feedback
Systems and Control.summary: Flexible AC Transmission Systems, particularly Static Synchronous Series Compensators (SSSCs), can increase the transfer capability of existing networks and complement constrained transmission expansion, but their value, optimal scale, and best locations in U.S. power system planning remain unquantified. This paper develops a capacity expansion model of the contiguous U.S. power system for 2050, incorporating SSSC-modified power flow equations. Expanding a line by adding parallel circuits lowers its equivalent impedance and, for a given SSSC rating, the series voltage the SSSC can inject. Through this transmission feedback, line flows depend nonlinearly on capacity decisions, making the planning problem nonconvex. We solve it by sequential linear programming (SLP) with adaptive proximal regularization. We prove the convergence to a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker point, which does not hold for the conventional fixed-impedance iteration. We also demonstrate that SLP converges faster to lower-cost plans. In the baseline scenario, the least-cost plan deploys 291 GVAr of SSSCs across the contiguous U.S. SSSCs reduce annualized system cost by $6.75 billion (2.1%) with an overall benefit-cost ratio (BCR) of 6.4 and lower the average wholesale electricity price by 5.1%. Alternatively, SSSCs could avoid about 75% of the transmission expansion without increasing system cost. Most of the economic value of SSSCs could be delivered by deployment in high-value locations: the highest-value 1 GVAr, located mainly near Eastern U.S. load centers, yields a BCR above 100, and one-tenth of the optimal SSSC capacity captures half of the savings. The overall BCR of SSSCs ranges from 4.1 to 9.1 across the demand, decarbonization, and device cost scenarios considered.

Systems and Control.title: Time to AC-t: When AC-transmission changes capacity expansion planning
Systems and Control.summary: Capacity expansion models often dramatically simplify the physics of how power flows through a transmission network in order to preserve computational tractability. However, with the rapid growth of electrification, large loads, renewables, and storage, increased realism in planning future grids is imperative. We extend the open-source capacity expansion model GenX with AC optimal power flow physics, and analyze generation, storage, and transmission investment decisions for 20-zone, hourly models of Germany and Texas. We compare our results against those using two common approximations, the transport model and DC optimal power flow. We find that total costs and emissions largely agree across all formulations. However, we find substantial differences in outputs related to transmission, generation siting, storage, and reactive-power support between the approximate formulations and the true AC physics formulation. We identify where AC physics changes planning decisions and discuss how to potentially capture these effects without the full computational cost.
Systems and Control.comment: 35 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables; plus 16 pages of supplemental information (8 figures, 6 tables). Submitted to Joule

Systems and Control.title: Methods for Accelerating and Stabilizing Nonlinear Magnetic Equivalent-Circuit Analysis
Systems and Control.summary: Design and optimization of electromagnetic devices require models that converge reliably and quickly and can represent intense localized magnetic saturation. This paper presents a parameterized 2D nonlinear magnetic equivalent circuit (MEC) and proposes solution methods for it: an approximate Jacobian that is symmetric positive definite, so each Newton-Raphson iteration can use sparse Cholesky factorization with fill-reducing reordering, and Anderson mixing as step control. These methods are compared with alternative nonlinear iterations, linear solvers, and step-control methods in convergence, computational cost, and prediction accuracy. Radial-flux magnetic gears (RFMGs) with structural bridges serve as a challenging test case, because their thin bridges exhibit intense local saturation. The methods are evaluated on three bridged base designs and on 1,024 bridged designs, each paired with the same design without the bridge. On the base designs, Newton-Raphson iteration with the approximate Jacobian reached much lower residuals than fixed-point iteration, which converged for none of them. Sparse Cholesky factorization with reordering was the fastest linear solver tested. Across the 1,024 design pairs, full-step Newton-Raphson converged for 193 bridged and 564 bridge-free designs, whereas Anderson mixing converged for 1,003 and 1,022 and required fewer iterations. Bridged designs converged less often and more slowly under every method. The nonlinear MEC was 2.17 and 1.84 times faster than fixed-mesh nonlinear finite element analysis (FEA) in total computation time for the bridged and bridge-free populations. The median outer-rotor torque discrepancy relative to FEA was 0.22%, and the Spearman rank correlations of the design rankings were at least 0.9996.
Systems and Control.comment: 14 pages, 11 figures. v5: substantially revised and reframed around solution methods for the nonlinear MEC (SPD approximate Jacobian with sparse Cholesky; Anderson mixing), with new comparisons on 1,024 bridged/bridge-free magnetic gear design pairs. Timing and accuracy results supersede earlier versions

Systems and Control.title: A Review of Max-Pressure Traffic Signal Control Algorithms: State of the Art and Research Opportunities
Systems and Control.summary: Max-Pressure (MP) has emerged as a widely studied decentralized traffic signal control framework, thanks to its desirable theoretical properties and strong control performance. Early research on MP focused on improving control performance by exploring different variables of the traffic state for the definition of pressure. Subsequent studies expanded MP to incorporate the complexity of real-world transportation systems and emerging technologies. This paper provides a comprehensive review of these developments. The review first introduces the theoretical foundations of MP and examines early developments in movement weight definition. It then synthesizes major extensions for multimodal and multiscale network control, followed by recent developments in connected and automated vehicle (CAV) environments and the integration of MP with artificial intelligence (AI) and data-driven methods. Beyond summarizing existing approaches, this review examines their underlying assumptions, data requirements, implementation considerations, and practical limitations. Based on this comprehensive review, key research gaps and future directions are identified, including remaining limitations in the theoretical foundations of MP and the underexplored integration of autonomous vehicle control with the MP framework. Overall, this review provides a structured perspective on the evolution and current state of MP control and highlights opportunities for developing more proactive, robust, and practically deployable MP-based traffic control methods.

Systems and Control.title: Holonic Graceful Transitions Across Centralized, Decentralized, Distributed, and Local Control in DER-rich Cyber-Power Distribution System
Systems and Control.summary: The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) in distribution system necessitates adaptive coordination frameworks. These frameworks must remain optimal during normal operation and resilient under cyber physical disturbances. Existing coordinated control approaches are typically deployed as static architectures with limited ability to adapt when communication degrades, local instability emerges, and operating conditions become spatially heterogeneous. This work addresses the gap by proposing a DER service-independent edge autonomous holonic adaptive coordination framework. In this framework, each DER controller executes its own control actions and transitions among centralized, distributed, decentralized, and local autonomous coordination modes without always relying on static coordination commands from the grid operator. The framework preserves coordination continuity across modes by retaining local controller states while reconfiguring only the coordination topology, information exchange pattern, and fallback action associated with the active DER service. Graceful transitions are enabled through dwell timers, rate limiting, and safety overrides to prevent dynamic instability during mode changes. Volt VAR control is used as a representative distribution automation application to validate the proposed architecture in a cyber-physical Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testbed. The proposed approach is evaluated under diverse cyber-physical event-based scenarios, showing region-confined adaptation under localized disturbance, reduced coordination traffic during coordination switching, and node-confined mitigation under cyber attack through edge anomaly detection and neighbor-corroborated impact estimation.
Systems and Control.comment: The paper is rejected based on multiple reviewers due to major concerns. So the full paper need to be revised before new submission and will change more that 50% of the contents

Systems and Control.title: MusiSPARQ: Subscription-Aware Adaptive Resource Control for Musical Metaverse Services
Systems and Control.summary: The Musical Metaverse relies on distributed audio, visual, inference, and delivery functions deployed across heterogeneous edge-cloud resources. Queue-aware orchestration frameworks such as SPARQ jointly optimize service placement, routing, and resource allocation, but fix the execution regime of each resource in advance: it is either shared, favoring statistical multiplexing, or guaranteed, favoring performance isolation. This paper introduces MusiSPARQ, a subscription-aware control framework that promotes resource isolation from a fixed infrastructure attribute to a runtime decision. Each switchable resource is represented through coupled shared- and guaranteed-resource pools drawing from the same physical-capacity budget, and at each orchestration epoch the controller selects which class-specific service flows remain shared and which receive isolated capacity. The per-epoch decision jointly accounts for class-specific latency objectives, per-class maximum-latency limits, queueing stability, isolation cost, and switching overhead. In a dynamic virtual-concert scenario, MusiSPARQ reduces the Premium latency-target violation rate from 16.19% to 0.29% relative to fully shared execution, while reserving on average only 0.71% of capacity and, unlike static isolation, keeping Standard and Basic traffic within their latency targets.
Systems and Control.comment: 10 pages, 9 figures. Accepted and Presented at IEEE International Symposium on the Internet of Sounds (IS2) 2026

Systems and Control.title: When Music Needs Meaning: Semantic Communication as a Transformative Enabler for the Musical Metaverse
Systems and Control.summary: The Musical Metaverse (MM) enables geographically distributed musicians, audiences, sound engineers, and AI agents to interact through synchronized audio, visual, kinematic, and haptic streams, imposing latency, synchronization, bandwidth, and scalability requirements that are difficult to satisfy with conventional bit-level communication. This paper argues that semantic communication, understood here as the transmission of musically meaningful information rather than raw audio-visual-haptic samples, provides a principled communication paradigm for the MM. We define the MM from a communication perspective and derive modality-specific require ments; propose a three-pillar framework for musical semantic communication comprising semantics extraction, semantic-aware orchestration, and cross-modal semantic synchronization; survey representative work across semantic communication, music AI and edge orchestration, identifying the gaps that prevent their integration; and propose a semantic-first reference architecture based on device-side semantic encoders, edge semantic routers, and cross-modal semantic synchronization. The resulting framework positions the MM as a concrete and demanding use case for 6G semantic communication.
Systems and Control.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Accepted and Presented at IEEE International Symposium on the Internet of Sounds (IS2) Conference 2026

Systems and Control.title: Contingency-Aware Planning via Certified Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability
Systems and Control.summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides formal safety guarantees for dynamical systems, but repeatedly solving the HJ partial differential equation in changing environments limits its use in real-time planning. This paper introduces learning-based reachability and an online safety certification that together enable real-time contingency-aware planning in unknown environments with probabilistic safety guarantees. We use Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) to approximate the HJ solution operator under varying obstacle configurations. To certify the learned reach-avoid set, we recast robust scenario optimization as multiple hypothesis testings over its sublevel sets, which yields a simultaneous guarantee across candidate levels and recovers the largest certifiable volume at the prescribed safety level. Within this certified set, the induced recovery policy is guaranteed to return the system to a safe region in finite time under any admissible disturbance. Numerical results show that the learning and certification pipeline updates reach-avoid sets at real-time rates and is demonstrated on youBot simulation.

Systems and Control.title: Model-Based Koopman-Galerkin Lifting for Guaranteed H-Infinity Output Feedback Control of Nonlinear Systems
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we present a model-based Koopman-Galerkin framework for output-feedback control of nonlinear systems with known dynamics. With a suitable actuator augmentation, the finite-dimensional realization preserves the actuator dynamics and the constant input matrix. The approach is based on an exact decomposition of the lifted dynamics into an LTI system and a finite-order closure residual. It also applies to non-control-affine systems and allows dictionaries that do not span an invariant subspace. Regional bounds are derived for the closure residual, actuator-realization defect, and output-reconstruction error. We use these bounds to formulate a standard $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ output-feedback problem. The controller is linear and dynamic and is implemented using only the measured tracking error. Neither full-state measurements nor a separate state observer are required. Lifting is performed offline. With the state coordinates retained in the dictionary, we obtain explicit transient bounds on the original state and tracking error. A sufficient condition for regional containment is also given. Under this condition, the nonlinear closed loop is forward complete, and the state and tracking error are uniformly ultimately bounded. The cart-pendulum example illustrates the nonlinear closed-loop guarantees. The proposed output feedback gives lower RMSE and peak tracking error on average than Jacobian-based $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ feedback, full-state backstepping, and Koopman-based hybrid MPC.

Systems and Control.title: A Modular Open-Source Python Framework for Small Satellite Attitude Determination and Control
Systems and Control.summary:
Advanced attitude determination and control (ADCS) techniques can be difficult for small satellite teams to adopt: tightly coupled implementations require substantial code changes to evaluate different actuators, sensors, orbits, mission goals, and control laws. Existing tools often emphasize orbit mechanics or flight software rather than closed-loop ADCS. This paper presents an open-source, modular ADCS framework in pure Python for rapid development, repeatable testing, and flight-oriented integration across heterogeneous spacecraft.
  The package supports torque- and command-level control, bound-respecting allocation, and full- and reduced-attitude objectives. Interchangeable estimation, control, planning, and actuator/sensor modules are reconfigured through configuration changes. Integrated simulation includes attitude and orbit propagation, sensor and actuator bias and noise, and environmental disturbances. An actuator-aware planner supports underactuated architectures, while hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) capability enables testing on mission-representative computers.
  Case studies include a 3U CubeSat with three magnetorquers and one reaction wheel, a magnetorquer-only 1U, and a 6U with three reaction wheels and thrusters. These demonstrate actuator and sensor failures, full- and reduced-attitude goals, and momentum management. HIL testing on a Raspberry Pi uses the same package. Adapting a published control law to a new actuator configuration requires fewer than five lines of configuration changes. The framework underpins flight software for an Earth-observing CubeSat with visible and long-wave infrared imagers, three magnetorquers, and one reaction wheel, without star trackers or propulsion.

Systems and Control.title: A Quantitative Approach to Reach-Avoid Reachability Analysis for Discrete-Time Nonlinear Control Systems
Systems and Control.summary: A reach-avoid specification requires a dynamical system to reach a target set of states while avoiding a failure set. Reachability analysis partitions the state space into parts starting from which the specification can be satisfied by following some control signal and those from which it cannot despite the best control effort. In this paper, we present a quantitative approach for reachability analysis to analyze the satisfaction of avoid and reach-avoid specifications for discrete-time nonlinear control systems. In such an approach, a value function assigns a value to each state that determines how robustly the system can satisfy the specification starting from it and following the optimal control signal. However, computing such a value function is difficult. Instead, our approach constructs discrete abstractions on which it performs value iteration to compute sound bounds on the desired value function. The resulting lower bound enables a sound under-approximation of the reach avoid set (RAS) and, in the avoid case, a sound over-approximation of the backward reachable set (BRS). When the control set is finite, the upper bound additionally enables a sound over-approximation of the RAS and, in the avoid case, a sound under-approximation of the BRS. The lower bound also yields quantitative guarantees on safety margins and safe target-reaching times. Our approach further refines the abstraction by splitting the grid cells that could not be classified as within or outside the BRS (or RAS) to improve the usefulness of the bounds. We evaluate our approach on five example systems with up to five-dimensional state spaces.

Systems and Control.title: Timely Ground-Station Status Delivery via UAV-Assisted Data Collection and Hierarchical RL
Systems and Control.summary: We consider a UAV-assisted status-update system in which a rotary-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) collects updates from multiple sensors, stores the newest update of each sensor, and forwards selected buffered updates to a ground station (GS). We minimize a weighted sum of the time-average GS-side age of information (AoI) and UAV energy consumption over a finite horizon. The optimization is subject to half-duplex operation, sensor and UAV energy-causality constraints, transmission-rate and power limits, and a terminal-location constraint. Because collection changes the information age at the UAV but does not reduce the GS-side AoI until the buffered update is forwarded, mobility, collection, and forwarding decisions are coupled over time. We use a hierarchical AoI-energy actor-critic (HAE-AC) controller in which a coarse-timescale actor selects return-feasible UAV movements, while a deterministic per-slot scheduler constructs feasible collection or forwarding sets and assigns the minimum transmit power required for each scheduled transmission. In a 100-sensor deployment, HAE-AC reduces the average GS-side AoI by about 22% relative to an adaptive staleness-gated benchmark. Compared with forward-upon-collection, selective buffered forwarding reduces the number of downlink bursts by roughly 30% while increasing the number of collections per sensor by more than 23%.
Systems and Control.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Author's accepted manuscript. Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 2026 Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems, and Computers

Systems and Control.title: Trajectory and Morphology Planning for Morphing Quadrotors in Ultra-Narrow Passages using Limited Perception
Systems and Control.summary: This paper presents an online trajectory and morphology planning framework for morphing quadrotors to traverse passages narrower than their unfolded width using only a 2D LiDAR for obstacle sensing. Fixed-frame vehicles cannot pass through such gaps, and classical artificial potential field (APF) based obstacle costs seal them off for planners as well, because the repulsive cost grows sharply inside a tight gap. The core enabler of our framework is a novel cost reduction factor, computed in closed form from the LiDAR data, that cancels the obstacle cost along the medial axis of a narrow passage. A true opening thus becomes a low-cost corridor, while the full repulsive cost is retained everywhere else. The cost reduction factor is embedded at every prediction node of an acados-based nonlinear MPC, which jointly plans the trajectory, yaw, and fold angle of the platform. A user-specified minimum-width limit ensures that the cost reduction factor only opens the corridors that the platform can actually pass. Gazebo/PX4 simulations and hardware experiments on the MorphoCopter demonstrate autonomous folding and unfolding through curved, inclined, and cluttered passages narrower than the unfolded width, where the standard repulsive cost fails to pass safely in most of the trials. The implementation code is available at \href{https://github.com/harshjmodi1996/morphocopter_mpc}{\textcolor{blue}{Github}} and a short video about the paper is available at \href{https://zh.engr.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/310/2026/10/Morphocopter_planning_final.mp4}{\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{video link}}}.

Systems and Control.title: A Tutorial on Shape Servoing of Deformable Objects-Part II: Advanced Concepts
Systems and Control.summary: In robotics, shape control, or shape servoing, refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object toward a desired shape. This article is the second of a two-part tutorial on data-driven, Jacobian-based shape control, in which the deformation Jacobian, a local model of how robot motion changes the measured shape, is estimated from measurements. Part I built the shape-servoing loop and derived a local stability condition. This paper starts by using the singular value decomposition of the deformation Jacobian to identify shape changes that can be produced by small robot motions, those that require large robot motions, and those that are locally unavailable. It then analyses how the choice of shape features determines how the controller regulates the object's shape and, therefore, how much the object deforms on its way to the target. It then describes three ways in which the shape control loop can fail: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and occurrence of mechanical instabilities. It closes with shape-control extensions to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.
Systems and Control.comment: Part II of a two-part tutorial. 10 pages, 9 figures. Code: https://github.com/nachocz/tutorial_on_shape_servoing_of_deformable_objects. Interactive demos: https://nachocz.github.io/tutorial_on_shape_servoing_of_deformable_objects/

Systems and Control.title: Adaptive Low-Rank Quantum Kernel Acquisition under Finite-Shot Measurements: Perturbation Guarantees for QSVMs
Systems and Control.summary: Quantum kernel methods require estimating entries of a dense Gram matrix through repeated circuit measurements, making kernel construction expensive and statistically noisy. For a dataset of size $n$, dense construction requires $O(n^2)$ kernel queries, while existing approximation methods typically assume inexpensive access to kernel entries or use non-adaptive sampling. We study adaptive low-rank quantum kernel acquisition when the kernel is accessible only through a finite-shot quantum overlap oracle. Our framework, ICAQKL, uses residual-driven incomplete Cholesky construction to acquire informative kernel columns sequentially and form a positive-semidefinite rank-$r$ surrogate, reducing the training-kernel acquisition cost to $O(nrN_s)$ circuit executions for $r\ll n$, where $N_s$ is the number of shots per queried entry. The central difficulty is that finite-shot errors perturb both the queried kernel values and the adaptive pivot sequence that determines the low-rank factor. We develop a non-asymptotic perturbation framework for this stochastic adaptive process, establishing concentration over the realized queries, stability of noisy pivot selection and factor construction, and propagation of the coupled sampling and approximation errors to the QSVM objective, optimizer, prediction function, and classification margin. The resulting rank--shot conditions characterize when ICAQKL approaches the full QSVM induced by the same quantum feature map. Experiments on benchmark and biomedical datasets show favorable accuracy--query-cost tradeoffs, competitive performance with the full QSVM, and competitive or improved performance relative to the evaluated Nyström baselines under comparable settings. ICAQKL is intended to enable measurement-efficient and theoretically controlled use of a selected quantum kernel, rather than to establish quantum advantage over classical kernels.

Systems and Control.title: ISAC-Assisted Proactive Handover in mmWave Networks: Value of Foresight and Localization Requirements
Systems and Control.summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) links can lose tens of decibels within milliseconds when a person or vehicle crosses the line of sight, and reactive handover recovers only after the outage has begun. Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) promises to let the network see blockers coming and move users to another cell in advance. This paper asks how much such foresight is worth relative to the best reactive handover, and what sensing accuracy is needed to harvest it. We formulate cost-aware cell selection with knowledge of the future signal-to- noise ratio as a sequential decision problem, define the value of foresight through a policy-independent bound, and develop an ISAC-assisted handover framework in which a radio unit senses blockers with its own communication waveform and a simulated Open RAN xApp plans handovers. Ray-traced experiments in a 28 GHz street canyon, reported on held-out scenarios, show that, with a short look-ahead, perfect foresight closes most of the gap between service-aware (Layer-3) reactive handover and an instantaneous oracle. Harvesting this value, however, requires the user and nearby blockers to be localized to about a decimeter, well beyond what our radar tracker and meter- level user positioning provide; with realistic errors, even an uncertainty-aware planner largely defers to reactive handover.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: When the Text Is Silent: Memory Shortcuts and the Validity of LLM Annotation under Evidence Insufficiency
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate text for social science research, content moderation, and training data. Their broad knowledge of real-world entities raises a concern: when labeling a text, do they rely on its evidence or substitute what they already know? We call this behavior a memory shortcut and examine when it emerges, what amplifies it, and how to mitigate it. Using 995 widely recognized public figures and four matched control names per figure, we construct counterfactual texts that separate textual evidence from prior knowledge, and evaluate three commercial LLMs on 121,594 prompts each across five stages. We find a striking asymmetry. Although all models recognize nearly every figure, none follows memory over the text when the two conflict. Shortcuts instead emerge when evidence is absent: for one model, famous names raise the rate of remembered occupations, ages, and countries by 17.0, 14.9, and 6.8 percentage points relative to synthetic names. These effects occur only for recognized figures, and 98.6% of the resulting labels are factually correct about the namesake while none is supported by the text. Evaluation threats and answer-contingent rewards amplify shortcuts by 8.7 and 12.4 points. Famous names also raise leadership ratings of sparsely documented applicants by 0.22 and 0.28 points in two models. A namesake reminder and name masking each eliminate the shortcuts, with trade-offs in gender annotation. LLM annotations can thus be factually correct yet methodologically invalid. Trustworthy LLM annotation requires audits that test evidence absence, account for incentives in annotation instructions, and evaluate the attribute-specific trade-offs of mitigation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 15 pages, 5 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: User Engagement in Visualization: A Scoping Review of 243 Research Articles
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: User engagement is well studied in other domains. Work to date has proposed conceptual models and definitions, approaches to measurement, and factors that influence engagement in digital interactions. However, of the articles in the visualization literature that refer to engagement, few of them make evidence-based, generalizable claims, and research that does is challenging to locate due to inconsistent reporting and often lacks connection to the broader engagement literature. To address these issues and promote the consideration of the broader engagement literature, we conduct a comprehensive scoping review of visualization literature and engagement. Using scoping review methodology, we identify and analyze 243 articles that make claims about engagement with visualizations. We coded the studies conducted, literature cited, definitions provided, and claims made in these articles and analyze the codes to evaluate the quality of the work in the field and to synthesize existing findings. We find that, despite frequent references to engagement and apparent interest in the topic, the overall quality of visualization engagement research is poor, often with weak evidence, inconsistent conceptualizations, and infrequent citation of existing models, methods, or claims. We report the evidence-based claims about what engages people with visualization, including the factors of animation, interaction, and immersion, additionally describing both corroboration and apparent contradictions between these claims. Finally, we propose the COMFI framework and mnemonic for reporting important information in future engagement studies.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "It just kind of shows that I went somewhere": An Exploratory Study of Fitness Data Visualization Sharing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The sharing of curated fitness data posts occurs frequently on fitness-focused social platforms such as Strava and on general social media platforms such as Instagram, which is a novel context for visualization. To better understand the process of sharing and designing fitness data posts, as well as the role of visualization within them, we conduct 18 semi-structured interviews with fitness data sharers. From our thematic analysis of the data, we find three novel characteristics for visualization through our study of fitness data sharing: (i) the role of visualization as proof, (ii) the tension between individuality and conformity, and (iii) the complexity of design decisions with regards to effort and desire to share. We also discuss a set of design implications, including a need for more options for visualizations for activities without routes, more user control in fitness data sharing platforms, and maintained ease of use while increasing customization options.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Harassment on TikTok: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Video Content and Psycholinguistic Comment Stances
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Despite extensive research on harassment, how it manifests on short--form video platforms such as TikTok---and how it shapes user interactions---remains underexplored, though these dynamics are critical for designing effective safety strategies for online communities. We present a mixed-methods study of 190 TikTok videos tagged with hashtag harassment and their 66,337 comments. Our qualitative analysis of videos identifies harassment types (sexual, verbal, stalking, law enforcement, bullying, catcalling, and gaslighting) and their characteristics (e.g., location, target, video style, and theme), along with engagement patterns. Although sexual harassment was the most prevalent topic, it did not have the highest engagement; instead, stalking--related videos received the most views. Pairwise comparisons and regression--based analyses of comments' psycholinguistic features and stance (support, opposition, neutrality) revealed differences in emotional tone, social orientation, and cognitive categories across harassment types. Comments on sexual harassment frequently express solidarity with victims, whereas discussions of law enforcement harassment emphasize institutional critique. We provide implications of our findings, demonstrating that harassment on TikTok is multifaceted, shaped by content, context, and community norms.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 34 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Review to Reuse: How Post-Task Workflow Can Support Human-AI Agent Interaction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI agents can automate tasks by turning a single natural-language request into a multi-step process spanning tools, files, and applications. Users are often left to judge that process from fragmented execution information and the final output. To make the completed process easier to understand, validate, and reuse, we investigate post-task workflows: editable, graph-based representations of an agent's completed execution. We first analyzed 10,803 public workflow templates from n8n to characterize real-world automation practice, then developed Trace2Flow, a research probe that translates agent execution traces into interactive post-task workflows. In a study, participants (N = 20) reviewed agent executions with prompt or agent errors. We found that post-task workflows improved their understanding and error detection over a prompt-only condition, and that validation succeeded mainly when users cross-checked across multiple evidence sources. For follow-up tasks, adapting the workflow matched adapting the prior prompt in success, time, and difficulty, and was often preferred.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: v2: supplementary appendix (survey questions, study materials) added as ancillary file

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Perception-Augmented Databases for Effective Visual Analytics
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Analysts often use sampling in visual exploration to overcome the computational and perceptual bottlenecks of working with massive datasets. Yet, existing sampling methods optimize for statistical or geometric data properties, without explicit consideration for how humans perceive a visualization. We propose perception-augmented databases: a database framework that stores perceptual models of data as precomputed metadata and exposes a new query operator---perception-aware sampling---that selects subsets optimized for how humans visually perceive the result. We make the following contributions: (1) We introduce perception-augmented databases and design PAwS, a perception-aware sampling operator for scatterplot visualizations that leverages saliency maps---a computer vision tool for predicting areas of visual attention---combined with density and coverage objectives. (2) We design ApproPAwS: a fast approximate visualization method that works directly over a perception-aware compressed synopsis of the data, achieving up to 100x speed-ups with minimal loss in visual fidelity, and without accessing the underlying data at query time. (3) We contribute a perceptual similarity metric that evaluates the quality of a sample by comparing its saliency map to that of the original dataset, a novel evaluation methodology, applicable to any sampling method for scatterplots. (4) Our extensive experimental evaluation over datasets up to 3.5M points demonstrates that our methods consistently outperform five state-of-the-art sampling algorithms. A user study confirms that PAwS samples are preferred by humans, validating our quantitative findings.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Capable but Not Scalable: Requirements and Interaction Costs of Building Multi-View CAD Datasets for Design Research
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Transforming CAD models into consistent multi-view image datasets is increasingly important for AI-driven product design research, yet existing workflows can impose substantial burdens on researchers without programming expertise. We examine this challenge from a human-computer interaction (HCI) perspective by analyzing ten reported rendering practices and deriving fourteen requirements spanning dataset quality, visual consistency, and user interaction. We then assess eleven development- and design-oriented tools against an illustrative task involving STEP models, interpreting potential interaction costs through the cognitive dimensions framework. Our analysis reveals a gap between technical capability and practical scalability: programming-based frameworks offer flexible automation but require coding expertise, while graphical design tools provide accessible functionality yet retain repetitive per-product operations. No assessed workflow combines a low programming threshold, low repetition viscosity, and flexible protocol configuration. Based on these findings, we propose design directions including reusable rendering presets, collection-wide previews and corrections, mixed-initiative orientation assignment, and automatic provenance recording. This work reframes CAD dataset generation as an end-user interaction design problem and establishes requirements for more accessible, scalable dataset creation tools.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Measuring "Success" In the Transition from Pre- to Post-LLM Conversational Agents through the Lens of Interaction & Explanations for Older Adults
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Conversational agents (CAs) for older adults have moved through at least two distinct eras, split by the emergence of large language models (LLMs) at the end of 2022. The first era was defined by commercial smart speakers such as the original Google Home and Amazon Alexa, built on rigid, rule-based dialogue. Interactions were single-turn, user-initiated and "successful" if and only if a command matched one of a finite set of pre-templated intents. The current era is marked by LLM-powered systems capable of open-ended, multi-turn conversation, with capacity for personalization and foundations for more proactive interaction. This shift has not only transformed what CAs can do for users, but also changed what researchers can measure when it comes to understanding "success" of user interactions with CAs. In this case study, we reflect on over 8 years of research spanning more than 100 participants across multiple field sites to trace how our own working definitions of "success" have evolved. We reflect on two completed bodies of work with pre-LLM CAs and an in-progress study with a post-LLM CA. We discuss how our definition and measurement of success have evolved during this transition and also ask open questions to the community about how to optimally measure "success" in the post-LLM CA era. This research is deeply applied and subject to the messiness of real-world deployments. Our intended contributions are deliberately practical, a combination of methodological considerations and reflection questions to support researchers engaging with this new wave of technologies.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted by GROUP Companion '27

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Feed-forward active magnetic shielding
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Measurement of small magnetic fields requires shielding. For example, magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures small fields arising within the brain, in the presence of environmental fields several orders of magnitude larger. A common solution is passive shielding, but its cost, bulk and limited effectiveness motivate the alternative approach of active shielding, which comes in two flavours: feed-back and feed-forward. In feed-back shielding (the most common design), coils are driven from sensors that measure the corrected field. In feed-forward shielding (less common), coils are driven from sensors that measure the uncorrected field. The latter has the potential of providing better performance, but its implementation is hobbled by an inevitable coupling between coils and reference sensors. This paper describes an approach that employs a data-driven ``decoupling matrix" to suppress the coupling, enabling greater flexibility to achieve effective shielding across a wide frequency range. The method is evaluated by simulation, first using a simplified "flat world" in which the principle is clearly visualised, and then based on the more realistic geometry of a standard MEG system. Performance appears to be limited only by spatial sampling and numerical resolution. The method, which is data-driven and does not require geometric calculations, tight-tolerance fabrication, or manual calibration, is complementary with standard feed-back shielding methods. Active shielding is of particular interest in the context of a new generation of optically-pumped magnetometers (OPM), as the lower cost and reduced constraints of these new systems relative to SQUID-based systems provide an incentive to likewise reduce the cost and constraints of shielding.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Vibe Paradox: What EEG Reveals About Your Brain When Vibe Coding
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Background: Much of the enthusiasm for vibe coding rests on two intuitive beliefs: (1) that developers stay invested even when they no longer write the code, and (2) that delegating more of the work to AI lowers their cognitive load. Objective: Our goal was to investigate whether developers' neurophysiological states and interactions with AI are consistent with these beliefs when they work with agentic vs. non-agentic AI on their own project vs. a legacy codebase.
  Method: We conducted an exploratory within-subjects crossover study with 11 participants across 22 sessions. Each participant used GitHub Copilot Chat in one session and Cursor Agents in the other, working on their own project and a legacy codebase, with tool-codebase pairings randomly assigned and session order counterbalanced. We recorded participants' EEG, on-screen activity, and prompts, and analyzed 7,924 EEG data points, 984 activities, and 141 prompts.
  Results: Our findings contradict both beliefs. With the agent, participants remained indifferent to task outcomes, even on their own projects, and cognitive load was higher than with non-agentic AI. Furthermore, their ways of interacting shifted: with non-agentic AI, participants asked how the code worked and read it to verify changes; with the agent, they described desired app behavior and checked results in the running app.
  Conclusion: Our study reveals a vibe paradox: delegating to an agent left participants motivationally disinterested, even on their own projects, without relieving cognitive load, while coinciding with increased trust in AI. The community should treat this paradox as a first-class concern if developers and their AI agents are to go far together, and not just fast.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Olivia Schutz and Rudrajit Choudhuri are co-first authors and have contributed equally

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EyeAgent: An Agentic AI System for Multimodal Clinical Decision Support in Ophthalmology
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Current medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems are often task-specific, poorly integrated, and difficult to interpret, limiting support for multimodal clinical workflows. We developed and evaluated EyeAgent for ophthalmic decision support. EyeAgent comprises three layers including 54 task-specific EyeTools, 32 clinical skills, and a modular large language model reasoning core with interchangeable backbones. A multi-level evaluation distinguished this scope from empirical system-level validation. Component-level evaluation assessed newly developed models on held-out splits of datasets totaling 871,862 samples. System-level evaluation included illustrative cases of workflow breadth, a 200-case expert-rating study of output quality, and an exploratory multicenter reader study comparing unassisted and EyeAgent-assisted performance among 27 ophthalmologists from 11 centers. Skill-level and backbone ablations further assessed orchestration and robustness. In illustrative cases, EyeAgent showed task-specific advantages over GPT-5.5 in lesion quantitation, cross-modality synthesis, and uncertainty-aware reporting. In the expert-rating study, EyeAgent achieved an F1 score of 0.84 for skill selection, with 82.7%-92.0% of outputs rated acceptable or better across six clinical dimensions. In the exploratory multicenter reader study, diagnostic accuracy increased from 72.8% unassisted to 91.9% assisted (difference, 19.1 percentage points (pp); 95% CI, 13.6-24.7; Holm-adjusted P<0.001). Report completeness increased from 55.8% to 75.6% (difference, 19.8 pp; 95% CI, 14.8-24.7; Holm-adjusted P<0.001). Across the evaluated settings, EyeAgent supported interpretable, evidence-guided reasoning and showed potential for human-AI collaboration. Broader real-world effectiveness and generalizability require prospective and cross-population validation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted for publication in NEJM AI

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Synthetic Realities: Evaluating Human Ability to Distinguish AIGenerated Videos from Real Footage
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Recent advances in generative AI have enabled multiple pathways for high-fidelity video synthesis: text-to-video, image-to-video animation, and video outpainting. Empirical side-by-side evaluations of how untrained viewers perceive and distinguish these outputs from real footage remain scarce. In this study, we systematically compare human detection accuracy across these three AI generation techniques within three thematic contexts: historical footage, film and media content, and natural environments. We constructed a balanced stimulus set comprising equal amounts of real and AI-generated videos (18 each). The AI clips were evenly distributed across the three generation methods using Google's Veo 3, Lightricks LTX Video, and Wan VACE. All videos were produced and standardized within the ComfyUI framework to ensure consistent quality and duration. 87 participants judged every clip in a binary forced-choice task ("real" vs. "AI-generated"). Participants correctly identified videos 60% of the time on average. Image-to-video clips were recognized most accurately (79%), followed by real footage (64%), outpainting (49%), and text-to-video (43%). Accuracy also varied by theme: film and historical scenes yielded higher detection rates than environmental clips, which were frequently mistaken for AI. Logistic regression confirmed significant effects of both technique and theme as well as their interaction (p < 0.001), indicating that detection success depends jointly on how the content was generated and what it depicts. Findings reveal a consistent bias toward assuming synthetic origins and highlight that perceptual realism in AI video is shaped more by context than by model type, underscoring the importance of media-literacy approaches and context-aware evaluation tools for navigating increasingly synthetic visual media.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Published in Proceedings of IASDR 2025

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Supporting Orthographic Recall of Chinese Characters through Self-Generated Compositional Mnemonic Stories: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Mnemonic studies on Chinese characters have mostly tested provided mnemonics against writing outcomes and self-generated mnemonics against meaning recall; whether writing one's own component-based story helps learners write the character has received little attention. I present Nuome, a tool that shows a character's component decomposition next to an editor in which learners write their own story, with live checks on whether the story covers every component and the character's meaning. In a within-subjects pilot, eight L2 learners each learned four self-chosen characters with the story builder and four with a read-only panel showing the same decomposition, with identical writing practice. Descriptively, partial-credit written-recall scores favoured the story builder by 18.8 percentage points immediately (N = 8) and 17.9 points after two days (N = 7); mean study time per character was 1.69 times as long (n = 6); usability was high (SUS 88.1). Interviews yielded three themes: participants felt that composing a story made them attend to components; knowing the components is not the same as being able to write them; and characters differ in how well they suit a story.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: TCLT13: The 13th International Conference and Workshops on Technology and Chinese Language Teaching, Oct 2026, The University of Hong Kong

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Interface Quilt: Modifying Applications with Computer Use Agents and Generative UI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Modifying an existing application is difficult when it does not provide programmatic access for that change. Recent advances in computer-use agents (CUAs) enable richer understanding and operation of existing interfaces, while generative UI (GenUI) makes it practical to generate new ones. We examine how these advances expand software modification through a design space of what can be changed and a framework for how modifications can be implemented. We then introduce Interface Quilt, a system that combines CUAs and GenUI to generate interface patches, which are new interfaces displayed over an existing application to modify its presentation, interaction, and capabilities. Through demonstrations across a variety of applications, we show that interface patches support a range of modifications without source code, APIs, or accessibility data.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Preprint, under review

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Graphs Have Structure: Declarative Manifolds, 3D Z-Order Monoid Roll-ups, and Zero-Simulation Visual Analytics in a Graph DBMS
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Every real-world graph is embedded in an ambient structural manifold: proteins fold in Euclidean space ($R^3$), telecom networks sit on a planetary surface ($S^2 \times R$), and ontologies and calendars form discrete subsumption posets ($(V, \sqsubseteq)$). Yet property graph databases treat node coordinates as opaque payload scalars, leave spatial proximity edges unindexed, and force visualizers into $O(V^2)$ client-side force-directed simulations that destroy true geometry and truncate hierarchy roll-ups. We elevate ambient manifold structure to a first-class primitive in Samyama Graph. First, we introduce a declarative and auto-detected structural convention contract (samyama.structure/1) persisted in .sgsnap headers that binds node labels to Euclidean 3D, Geo-Spherical, Causal Spacetime, or Poset Hierarchy manifolds. Second, we show that both discrete posets (via Order-Embedded Hierarchy $[tin, tout]$ DFS intervals) and continuous 3D manifolds (via a 63-bit 3D Morton Z-order Structural-Geometric Index, SGI) reduce regional aggregation to 1D rank-interval monoid folds answered directly from index-resident Fenwick trees (SUM, COUNT) and Segment Trees (MIN, MAX). At $100,000$ 3D nodes, SGI builds in $28.14$ ms and answers Morton-interval SUM and MAX roll-ups in $0.048\,μ$s and $0.104\,μ$s---$8,345.1\times$ and $3,824.4\times$ faster than property scans. Third, we introduce 3D voxel-hashed virtual contact edges weighted by Topological--Geometric Stress $σ(u,v) = d_{graph}(u,v) / d_{manifold}(u,v)$ to isolate long-range tertiary folds, plus manifold-guided $A^*$ shortest-path search that cuts explored states by up to $3.80\times$ over Dijkstra. Fourth, we replace client layout simulation with server-computed 3D Cone-Tree/Ribbon coordinates and a non-WebGL 2.5D Isometric projection with painter's-order depth sorting and sub-millisecond Level-of-Detail (LoD) macro-cuts.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Companion to arXiv:2606.24677 (OEH). Code: https://github.com/samyama-ai/structural-manifold-index and https://github.com/samyama-ai/samyama-graph/pull/2038

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MaterialVellum: Steering Generative AI by Leveraging Expressive Material Affordances to Form Design Constraints
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We present MaterialVellum, an interaction approach for steering generative AI through material-inspired manipulation of design constraints. In urban design, for instance, zoning bounds can be defined by the stretch of elastic bands, building density redistributed by molding clay, and functional relationships organized by the pull of magnets. MaterialVellum departs from current interfaces that rely on natural language prompts, and instead leverages users' existing knowledge of physical materials to represent and manipulate design constraints. We introduce a framework that maps material affordances---such as elasticity, malleability, or attraction---to spatial, relational, and proportional constraints that underpin design. These mappings are operationalized in user interfaces through familiar direct manipulation multi-touch gestures, including stretching, sculpting, and clustering, whose effects feed as control parameters into generative AI pipelines.
